utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have a witness to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are two witnesses who I expect we will deal with today, at least deal with one completely and one we'll deal with in part. To ensure that I don't forget outstanding issues, the witness who should have attended last week but didn't has been the subject of further enquiry. I'll be able to report, I think, after the week's break, more fully and with more direct information, what the position on that witness is and whether he is going to come here voluntarily or not. There are one or two other outstanding administrative matters, but I needn't deal with them now, but I would like to make sure I have a period of administration this week. The Chamber will not have forgotten the map that shows front lines that the Chamber had itself wanted, and there's questions of the preparing of not dossiers in respect of the village, the various villages and communities, but you will remember that I'm preparing and promised to have prepared by, I think, the end of October our final position on those matters, and you'll want to know how we're doing and whether the timetable is being kept to. I think it is, but I've got all those matters in hand. As to the witness today, the first witness seeks protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do that, while I have it in mind, let me mention this: Friday morning has presented a difficulty in that one of our number is sitting on another trial, or another matter, I should say, not a trial. It's not known how long that's likely to be. It's listed for 10.00. Rather than having everybody here, hoping we can start sometime that morning, it seems simpler to cancel that morning's hearing, so there will be no hearing on Friday. I recognise that these matters cause difficulty, but the fact is we are all engaged in other cases. It's a factor or a feature of our practice. You've got, according to the note we have, four witnesses listed for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you anticipate, if we make reasonable progress, we shall be able to deal with those?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's a bit optimistic to think we'll deal with all four, but we'll see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've planned provisionally on the basis that the fourth might have to be kept over the weekend, in any event. That was allowing for a start by Thursday or Friday, but let's see how we go. The first witness seeks protection. An application was served last week. The protection sought would be limited to pseudonym and distortion of the face. We're not in private session at the moment. To go into it further might require private session, but it may be that the application is not opposed. I'm not sure. Not that that determines it. It's a matter for the Chamber, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Dario Kordic has no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour, the Defence of Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I only make this comment: When we started this case, we said that these matters should not be routine. I can't help but notice that most of the last witnesses, those that have been called since the break, some 12 or so, 13 perhaps now, about nine have asked for these measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Sir. All I can say on that is, as I noted at the beginning of the case, certainly it isn't routine for us to seek protection. On the contrary, each and every witness is the subject of full explanation as to the desirability of matters being heard in public, and indeed save for a very limited number of witnesses, I've dealt with this matter myself before allowing an application for protection to come to the Court. That explanation having been made to the witness, of course, if the witness seeks protection, it's our duty to transmit that request to your Chamber, and the Chamber will have noted that to some extent the reaction of witnesses, understandably, is built upon their own experience indirectly, of what happens to other witnesses in this trial, so that if the Chamber looks to paragraph 3 in this application -- again I needn't spell out the details -- one can see -- sorry, paragraph 2 -- you can see that part of her concerns today arises from what has happened in respect of other witnesses in this trial, so that they come here with heightened anxiety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll make the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness can be fetched, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The blinds must, of course, be dealt with first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While that's being done, the summary arrived in good time, for which we are grateful. There does seem to be an amount of hearsay, and I have in mind paragraph 7, which we've heard a great deal about, paragraph 16, which we've heard about, and -- I'm sorry, paragraph 9 and paragraph 10. Then paragraph 16 to 18, this seems to me to be, and I speak entirely for myself, but this seems to me the sort of secondhand hearsay which I wonder how much assistance we derive from it. Perhaps you might like to consider, Mr. Nice, as you go through, whether it's necessary to rely on all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The first two points I had already excised effectively from the material I needed to lead. The last point is rather more important. Yes, we do seek to lead that material. The alternative, of course, would be to call a number of women, if they were willing to come, and expose them to the distress here. It's not the case that allegations are made in respect of these defendants specifically. It is the case that this part of the persecution count, that this material is important. The people to whom these women were complaining were professionals, and there being no rule against hearsay, it was our judgement that this was an important part of evidence to produce in this way. Here is the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym that will be used for this witness is Witness S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could look, please, at this piece of paper. Madam, will you just tell us yes or no, but yes if that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The blinds are being raised. I can start in order to save time. Witness S, have you set out on a -- or have you seen set out on a printed summary both your personal details and your occupation indeed as a doctor in Zenica and in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Vitez since qualifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to pass over paragraphs 1 to 3. At the time of the conflict were the majority of doctors in the Vitez health centre of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the Muslim director, Dr. Balta, or Balta, someone who had to resign, and was he replaced by a doctor of Croat ethnicity, Dr. Kajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were only minimal salaries paid, and there were problems with medical storage and restocking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time, in 1993, was a doctor of Croat ethnicity, Bruno Busic, appointed as minister of health in Vitez, and thereafter did he have considerable influence on the hospitals affairs, although not an employee of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 16th of April of 1993, were you at home when your landlord's son informed you of problems with Muslim houses being on fire and making allegations that some people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you remember now any of the names of people who were said to have been killed by your landlord's son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the names of Nedim and Mira, a married couple. I recall the name of Midhat Varupa. I recall the name of the police commander, Saban. I believe his last name was Mahmutovic, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nedim and Mira, can you recall their last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nedim and Mira, I cannot recall their last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if there is any objection. If there isn't, I'll lead it. If there is none, I'll go on. Does the name Zlotrg --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could be Zlotrg. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day did you go to work and discover that the health centre had moved locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you speak to a colleague, Dr. Drita Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was she able to tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said that her husband, a physician who was employed as a radiologist in the Travnik hospital, Ekrem Mahmutovic was his name, had been detained at the Workers' University, arrested, and that she used all her contacts by calling people on the telephone in an attempt to have her husband set free. And he was released and he went back to work in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did she name any of the particular people that she contacted and whose contacts had proved significant in having him released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only name which was familiar to me was the name of Mario Cerkez, which she mentioned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, what was his role in community life at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I know, Mr. Cerkez was the commander of the HVO brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he known to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following the attack, of which you learned on your return to the relocated health centre, were two Muslim doctors, Trako and Patkovic, brought to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were brought in several days after the conflict. I don't know exactly how many days. I couldn't tell you whether this was the 5th or the 4th day after the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were they brought to the hospital to carry on work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having previously been held where; did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was the Workers' University, that is in respect of one of them, and I believe that the other one said that he would voluntarily appear at work, probably in order to avoid being arrested. I think this was a more acceptable solution for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were various Muslim men brought to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat the question? I did not fully understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Were various Muslim men treated at the health centre thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were Muslim men who were treated at the centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what needs for treatment did they typically have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several men who had been wounded when they were digging trenches for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these men soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What type of injuries or wounds did they typically have, these trench diggers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them had a serious injury. I remember him. He was the husband of one of our medical nurses whose name was Zulejha.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a serious and complicated injury of the lower extremity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Caused by what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the only firearm wound that you saw on such men, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were Muslim women brought to and treated at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as they were wounded, what sort of wounds did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All caused by firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where had these women been, as you understood it, and learned before they were brought to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were brought to the health centre for examination, they told me something that -- well, I learned for the first time at that time that they had been placed in a house in Novaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long had they been at that house, did you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "yes" or "no" to this question. Apart from evidence of injury through firearms, did some of these women complain to you or did you learn of them complaining to other people of other types of injury that they had suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, insofar as any woman is going to be named as a victim of a different type of event, I would ask the Chamber to consider private session being appropriate, simply to protect those women's names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session for the next part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the end of 1993, were you ordered one day by the director of health, or the director of the health centre, to be one of a three-party commission, the other two members of that commission being Franjo Tibolt, the Croatian of whom you've spoken, and Rada Savanovic, a Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But this was not at the end of 1993. It was perhaps at the end of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite right. I think that's what I asked, and maybe it got missed in the translation or possibly it's my mistake, of which I apologise. The purpose of the commission, did it include the visiting of detainees in the cinema to check their health and to prepare a list of those who were to be released on medical grounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went to the cinema, were you able to enter the rooms where the detainees were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was possible to enter, but I didn't go in. They took us to the hall, a corridor, where there were tables and chairs set for the doctors to be able to examine the detainees, the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were those detainees brought to you in groups of three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came out three at a time and approached, one by one, one of the doctors, depending on who was free at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Come back to paragraph 24. When you saw the prisoners -- paragraph 27, 27 and 28 -- what condition were they in and what mental state did they appear to be in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that fear was the dominant impression, and uncertainty, yes, as to what would happen to them. My basic impression was that they were terrified and they didn't know what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did any of them express their fear or terror?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were mostly frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they say what they were frightened of, or were they frightened of what would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't tell me in so many words, but I think that they feared for their lives. They were uncertain about what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What age range were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were young and middle-aged, but there were some elderly too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see any particular injuries; for example, a broken arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There weren't any particular injuries among the prisoners who came to me to be examined, with the exception of one prisoner who was complaining that over the previous few days he had received a blow in his jaw, and he had an injury of the finger. He was hit by somebody whom he called by his nickname Cicin. And there was another prisoner who had an injury of the arm which had been immobilized, but he didn't come to me to be examined on that day. Probably he was examined by one of my colleagues, because I do not remember him from that day. But several days later, after this visit of ours to the Workers' University, my colleague Kajic, who was the manager, he asked me to write out the diagnosis for this person, as I was a member of this commission, together with colleague Tibolt, and that Bosko Pavlic, another colleague, should also sign, as he was head of the medical department. And it was then that I saw this person with his arm in a cast. I wrote out the diagnosis and I asked colleague Tibolt to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But his answer was that he didn't dare or, rather, that he would not sign, and that I should understand him. So that this report went off with my signature and colleague Pavlic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One last question on these two men. The first man you spoke of, the man who complained of being hit by the man who he knew by a nickname, what was the name of that man, the man who was injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Serif Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 27. Roughly how many prisoners did you meet on the day that you went to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be hard for me to give you a number, but a very rough indication, it may have been more or less, but I really don't know the number, but perhaps some 50 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people altogether did you see being checked up by you and your colleagues altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I must say that I am not sure of the figure. I may easily be mistaken, but my rough estimate would be between 100 and 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there -- paragraphs 24 to 26 -- was there a local Vitez television crew present for all or part of this day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they interviewing Dr. Tibolt about possible mistreatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was Tibolt's reaction to their questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question they insisted on, among others, was whether there were any traces of mistreatment. Tibolt's answer was that nobody had complained of that. That's what I do remember. And that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the effect of the broadcast, if you saw it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the effect was a propagandist one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 30. At the end of this exercise, was a report prepared and were some prisoners subsequently released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the end a report was compiled. My colleague, Ms. Savanovic and myself, dictated what we had found among the patients. We dictated the names and diagnosis to Tibolt. And just then a representative of the Red Cross appeared, who was also present during these examinations. He was sitting across the way from us, at some distance. And after he came, colleague Tibolt asked Dr. Rada and myself to leave, and he stayed on with this representative of the Red Cross to finish the report. So that I had no insight into those who were released, but I do know that some prisoners were released, but I don't know who, nor how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Red Cross representative who turned up, can you give us his name and his ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think his name was Stipo Krizanac, and he is a Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you went home. The people of the cinema were guarded by what type of soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 32. Did you see HVO soldiers at the hospital from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you notice any particular groups of soldiers identified by their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What I noticed, and I hadn't noticed before the beginning of the conflict, was a group of soldiers, mostly young men, wearing black uniforms with patches indicating Jokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did they behave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were noisier than others and they were considered more extremist than the HVO soldiers in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 34. Did you know a man named Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not personally. But I knew his face. I knew him by sight. And I think that he was a patient -- no, I don't think so. I know. I know that he was a patient of my colleague, Dr. Mujezinovic, who treated him for drug addiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he, that is, Darko Kraljevic, at one stage sign certificates in relation to the safety of houses for doctors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you, I think, took the view that you didn't need such a certificate for yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I came to work the next day, when the gentleman working in security offered to give me this certificate with my name on it and saying that I was an HVO doctor, with the signature of Darko Kraljevic on it, and I could refuse that because I felt partially protected, as I was in a Croat house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kraljevic himself, did you understand that he led a group, and if so, what was the name of the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the group was called Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Included in the HVO soldiers you met, paragraph 33, was there any who spoke English rather than a language native to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, a wounded Englishman who was in the HVO army came, and he had an injury in his mouth. But he was making a lot of noise and he would not allow us to approach him and to treat him, and he was armed, so that it was difficult to gain control over him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he spoke English. Did he say anything about where he came from, or did you learn anything about where he came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said he was an Englishman without thinking over the point properly. He spoke English, but I don't know where he came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he speak or appear to have any ability to speak your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not speak our language. But with him was a young woman, and they said that she was his girlfriend and interpreter. She was interpreting, and she tried to calm him down so that we could treat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, a word or so about your move from Vitez to Zenica. Can you help us with the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was May. I think it was the 16th or somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did it come --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did it come that you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. How did it come that you moved to Zenica? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left with the help of the UNHCR. I was assisted by a woman who had worked with me in the health centre and whose daughter was working in the UNHCR in Zenica. I was also assisted by a man, a Croat also, who drove me by car to the road near the company called Impregnacija, and the UNHCR came to pick me up, as arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give me the name of the two people, please, the woman and the man who helped you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The woman's name was Ljilja, and she was a laboratory technician in the health centre. I really do not remember her surname. And the man's name was Trpimir Vujica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went to the place, did you travel in a car or in some other type of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a passenger car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your knowledge of Dario Kordic, was that limited to what you saw on the television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Wait there, and you'll be asked some further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I will have some questions on cross, and we agree with other Defence that I will go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I please ask permission to move forward, because I cannot see the witness from here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm an attorney from Rijeka, and I represent the Defence of Mr. Cerkez here in court. I have to address you with your pseudonym, so I apologise for that in advance. Madam, you arrived in Vitez towards the end of the '80s, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were assisted by some colleagues when you arrived, in terms of finding a flat and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the greatest assistance was given to you by Mrs. Slavica Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that also is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were on good terms with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the health centre, inter-ethnic relationships were correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Slavica Cerkez was a nurse, wasn't she, and she worked with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And she's the wife of the accused here, Mr. Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, did you meet Mario Cerkez over the years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice any kind of prejudice or negative attitudes regarding ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To the extent to which I knew the gentleman, though I knew his wife better, I never noticed any such prejudices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask the Court -- I mean I'm asking permission whether we can show to the witness D19/2, which was the list of the employees employed in the health centre in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is only to confirm. If I recall correctly, Dr. Mujezinovic said, "Yes, that seems to be a proper list," and since this witness was employed there, perhaps it would be good that she checks so we know that we have a proper document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, an earlier witness, a colleague of yours, looked at this list. Will you please look at what is stated in the brackets below the heading, "List of workers employed in the Vitez Health Centre"? It says the period from the 1st of January until the 1st of June, 1993, so this is the first half of the year. So please look at this list, and will you confirm, are those the people who were employed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You can see from this list that there was a total of 13 doctors; isn't that so? Let me assist you. Under numbers 9, 24, 25, 26, 31, 32, 37, 38, 52, 65, 67, 68, 74, those are doctors that you have referred to during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember Dr. Dragana Rijec, I'm afraid, number 68. I can't recall Dragana Rijec, I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe she joined later on in June, when you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that roughly those are the people who were working in the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So judging by the names, at least, it follows that there was roughly the same number of doctors who were Muslims and Croats, I would say the ratio was six to six, and of course on the basis of surnames, probably two Serbs. Would that be correct? Would that correspond to your own impressions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can take that. Madam, you spoke about the new manager of the health centre, the appointment of Dr. Kajic. Could you tell us when that was exactly, or approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately January, 1993. I may be wrong. It may be a month before or later, but it was about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. And was that appointment lawful, in line with the then regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you remember if there was an employed meeting called on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But the assembly of workers was the highest management body in whatever company, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was workers assembly which decided to appoint Dr. Kajic as the manager?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there was nothing unlawful about that. In my testimony, I merely spoke about the resignation of colleague Balta, and rather than that colleague Kajic was elected unlawfully. He was -- everything was quite legitimate. But we were simply talking about the fact that he brought colleague Balta into a situation to submit his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion did you hear that Dr. Kajic was specially trained as a military surgeon for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that. Oh, excuse me. Excuse me. Dr. Kajic used to work, I believe in Sarajevo. No, that is true. I just never gave it a thought. Yes, he did work as an army surgeon there. Yes, quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, could you remember -- do you remember the time frame at least, was it then that the immediate war danger had already been proclaimed in the Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina, and is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So would it look natural to you that the staff and its ethnic composition was not remarkable in a way that they would appoint as a new manager a doctor who would perhaps be more knowledgeable about things that may happen in times of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as for the expert knowledge, colleague Balta is more experienced and he was a specialist; that is, if we are referring to the medical knowledge. I do not think that would be a good comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. You said -- rather, you answered the Prosecutor's question that salaries were at a very low level and the medical supplies were not replenished easily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that is what I wanted to ask you, so as to make it clear for people who do not come from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was the health centre an exception or was that the situation across the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation across Bosnia-Herzegovina was such; that is, salaries were a minimum and there was a shortage of medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And how about other health centres which you maintained some professional contact? Were they better off, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean, no. We might be discussing -- there were shades of shortage, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the situation was generally very bad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This situation was generally very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the situation was also bad, among other things, because due to the JNA's aggression at the time, this state had practically stopped functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the communications were bad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for the above-mentioned, Mr. Bruno Busic -- and you told us he was appointed minister of health care in the municipality of Vitez -- he was a dentist? He had his private surgery, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he also attended to the patients in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Busic was full-time employed with the health centre, and after that, I wouldn't know when exactly, '90 or when, but he left the health centre and he had his private surgery. He had his -- I don't know that he continued working in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in the health centre there was all the dental equipment and all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course there was. But after he became self-employed, I think he ended his contract with that health centre, but I didn't know when that was. It could have been 1990 or perhaps even '89. I wouldn't know that. But when I came to the health centre, he was still employed with it, and then he changed and started his private practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But this Mr. Busic, we are agreed about that, he was the minister for health care at the municipal level, in the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So could you, madam, tell us, please, wasn't that a matter of choice and posting, distribution among the parties which made up the municipal government, and then distribute among themselves various posts, various duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess it was that way, but I didn't really know much about those political things. I wasn't really in those political waters, but I guess that that must have been what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. You mentioned that people in the municipal administration, even though you said that was not the case at the health centre, that people signed a kind of statement of loyalty or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was when the municipal administration split into the Muslim and the Croat part. That was a common fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you have ever a chance to see what it was that they signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not get that at the health centre, so we don't know what they got. I heard what I heard, is that they were signing statement of loyalty to the Croat community of Herceg-Bosnia. That is what I heard, but I did not have an opportunity to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, please take care not to mention any names, so that we don't have to go into a private session. But you referred to several cases when you -- when you heard about rape by the -- either directly or indirectly. I should like to ask you the following: if in any of those cases whether you ever heard which soldiers raped those women.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean their names, or at least their membership of the units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. And in those stories did you ever hear that this or that rape was perpetrated by so-and-so, with a full name, or at least a member of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You never heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in all those rumours about all that, you never heard a thing like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really remember a name being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned a lady, and I won't mention her name, but you will remember who it was, who you said was kept in Novaci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean in those Bungalows, Bungalows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that is what you said about the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Quite right. That one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The one from Novaci. Do you know where Novaci is? Do you know the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly only, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you wouldn't be able to tell us which army held at Novaci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you don't know which unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you don't know who kept her there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And about those rapes, I should like to ask you just one more thing. In view of your profession and all of the developments in Bosnia, would you agree that in Central Bosnia, and in particular in the territory of the Vitez municipality, as you were there, rape was not a common feature or a widespread feature in that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. When I learnt about that, I was rather surprised. I do not think it was a widespread phenomenon, as against information, that is judging by what I know, what I could see. I can only, of course, speak about myself and my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I am referring to your assessment. So we can agree that there was such cases and you mentioned some of them that you learnt about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Nod].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it was not a general widespread phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the information that was available to me, it was not a widespread phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, what period are you referring to in these questions about rape being a widespread phenomenon? Are you talking about the period before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour. I should be more precise. Thank you for warning me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you perhaps ask the witness, first of all, whether it was widespread before the war, and then whether, in her experience, it was widespread during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, you heard the interpretation of this question. Could you tell us, when was it, prior to April 1993 when the conflict broke out, did you hear about any rapes that you could associate with the ethnic -- with the ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, I never heard of any case of rape that I would associate with somebody's ethnicity. After the conflict broke out, I heard about several cases, but I am a woman, and even those few cases are just -- are just one too many for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they are the ones that you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are the ones that I heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned when Mrs. Drita Mahmutovic, her husband was arrested, when she told you that she tried all her possible contacts to have her husband released, he was detained in Zenica, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, in Vitez. And among other things, she also said that she had sought Mr. Cerkez's assistance. And you said too that, "The only name familiar to me that she mentioned was Cerkez."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. She opened her address book and she was uttering various names, but I knew Cerkez's name because of his wife, because we worked together and cooperated. And other names she mentioned, but that name was familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that was what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were other names too, but they did not convey anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right, thank you. As a doctor, and I'm referring to '93 in the health centre, were you ever issued some labour directives at the health centre at any time in '93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, yes. I believe, yes, we were issued those directives. Yes, that is quite true. Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But would you agree that physicians and all the other medical personnel were assigned to those jobs which they were doing, anyway, as professionals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in the cinema building and examined a certain number of detainees, and that, in your view, they were all terrified, frightened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please, as a physician, in just two sentences, tell us, what were the objective criteria, that is, the medical standards, whereby you determined the presence of fear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this would fall into the psychiatric domain, but organically speaking, that is, somatic symptoms, what is material, what we can confirm, is hypertension, enlarged irises, tachycardia, excessive perspiration. Those are some of the symptoms. But the term "fear", it is more a psychological term. It is not really easy to define. It can be without all this, and one can assess it on the basis of an interview. The voice which sometimes trembles, which is perhaps too fast or too slow, the facial expression, these are things which are perhaps less palpable, less tangible, and more difficult to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have to wait for the interpreters. Bearing in mind those criteria and the circumstances, of course, which existed there, you, of course, could not establish what you would have been able to establish in your surgery, so there were some -- there were certain things that you could not establish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite true. Without the laboratory, without all the equipment, it's quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that fear, I mean strictly medically speaking, you could not prove that fear, could you, medically speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very difficult to prove fear, to have some tangible evidence, but it was -- yes, there were some medical cases, there were some of those signs that I mentioned before which are quite tangible, and there was fear, there was fear. I absolutely insist on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. You mentioned this man with his arm in a cast. The first time he was brought to this commission, you said not to you but to another doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he had been attended to? He had his arm in the cast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw him, he had already been treated. But when he was injured and when he was treated, I really don't know and I didn't really ask too much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps let's move on slower, and then perhaps we shall get at what we're aiming for faster. So when you saw him, it was for an additional medical examination, so he was being treated, he was receiving care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All the administrative parts of it had already been taken care of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During those examinations, during those check-ups in the cinema, apart from fear, which you explained to us, and this case of this patient with the arm and the like, but was there anything that would make you conclude that those people were really deprived of medical assistance, that they were neglected, that they were left without medical care, even though they needed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think there were any particular cases, except that there was a man, a younger man, who said he was a diabetic, but I believe that he was released that day, on that list. And other cases mostly suffered from various chronic diseases. A couple of people had some acute respiratory infections and things like that. But I think that fear was the predominant problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But could we agree, and I'm referring to the day which you saw in that part, as a doctor, as a physician, you will agree that it was not evident that it was a group of people which had been left without medical care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask the Court if we can show the witness the earlier presented evidence D20/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were on this commission and examined the -- and this list with Dr. Tibolt, will you please look at the signature at the bottom of the list and the names on the list? Could you please tell us if you examined any one of those 22 persons you recommended for release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's too difficult. I don't remember those names. I wouldn't really go into that. No, I don't remember names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right, madam. I will now ask you, at the bottom to the right, there's a signature. You did know the signature of your colleague signed "Tibolt". Was that his signature or not, from what you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you know, why is it that on the left-hand side we have the signature and then it says "Approved, Pero Skopljak"? What was his role there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was the police chief at the time or something. Pero Skopljak, Ministry of the Interior, or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished with this paper. After that, you mentioned, when you sat down to write those papers, you mentioned a certain Stipo Krizanac and said that he was the Croat representative of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the Muslim representative had also been detained in the university building. His name was Sead Cajnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But then he was released, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was released later on, but he was detained first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And would you know that Stipo Krizanac was also a representative of the civil authorities of the HVO there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, I really don't know. I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Serif Causevic, who had been hit by one Cicin. Did you hear anything about where that had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And incidentally, was Cicin a Croat or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know who it was by that nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, Cicin came to Emergency. I think he had quite a delinquent behaviour, quite rowdy. That is how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are we talking about Cicin or Cica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cicin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You spoke about labour directives, labour obligations. Did you know and was it true that under the regulations, you were not allowed to leave the territory of the municipality except by authorisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, regardless of any permits or authorisations, I think I would have tried to leave because my safety was at stake. Of course, I mean my safety comes first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I'm asking you simply -- I'm not asking you within the context; I'm simply asking you whether it is true that there was such an obligation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So nobody needed to tell you particularly, "Madam, you're now under work obligation and you have to stay here"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Because you already had this labour obligation before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Individuals who helped you leave Vitez, and you mentioned one Ljilja and Trpimir Vujica, they are both Croats, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This English-speaking soldier who came to you with his head injury to the health centre, you said he was with the HVO. Did you see any insignia on him, on the basis of which you would be able to conclude which unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, you didn't. But did he have any HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Dr. Tibolt made a statement on television, too, about the state of health of persons detained in the cinema and that he said that nobody complained of ill treatment in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he said, and it's true, nobody complained of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But nevertheless, madam, you used the term, if I am correct, that the fact that television recorded that examination as a form of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we might agree about that. But allow me to ask you if, in that particular story that you saw about it, was there anything untrue in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was nothing untrue, I didn't say that, but I simply saw it more as an advertisement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As an advertisement, you're saying. But did I understand you well: The HVO is bragging about they did well; they invited doctors to go in there? Was that how you saw that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To conclude, perhaps: You said that when you left Vitez, you spent a short while in Zenica, and then some time in summer you accepted a job and moved to Preocica, to the hospital, in the hospital kept by the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was Preocica. This was July '93. Yes. Escorted by UNPROFOR, I went as an army doctor to Stari Vitez beyond the line, and I stayed there until the Washington Accords, and that is until March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm asking too much, but I believe it would serve the common interest. A while ago, you said that regardless of the labour obligation, you left Vitez because you did not feel safe there and that your safety came first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But then in July, you went back to Stari Vitez, although it was surrounded, and it must have been very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So why did you, after all? Your safety ceased being your first concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now it was a matter of ethics. It was a matter of siding with the weaker, with the one who has to defend himself, and the feeling of patriotism, of pride, so that was a bit or all of that. Of course, yes, I was afraid too, but after all that I had seen and experienced, there was this wish to help to defend, to withstand. There was this defiance, to put up defiance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But that was a hospital, that was a medical base or whatever we call it in Stari Vitez. It was under the care of the army of BH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During that long period of time until the spring of '94, Stari Vitez was under blockade all that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a physician, did you manage, in cooperation with UNPROFOR and other institutions, but of course also with the authorisation of the HVO, you did manage to take patients out of that encirclement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not always, unfortunately. Very many lives were lost, and yet they did enjoy a certain chance because UNPROFOR could not enter because they would be stopped by the HVO, and they wouldn't insist. But yes, there were cases of when we evacuated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the situation fluctuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning -- in the beginning, they could enter more frequently, but as time went on, they were less and less frequently allowed to enter, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it's now past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm on my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right, your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree that until the end, until -- that it fluctuated; the situation fluctuated, didn't it, until the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Kordic has no questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was brief. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have two questions in re-examination. Shall I take those before the break, if that's acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'll deal with it briefly, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness S, two questions, I think, please, possibly three. The first question: The replacement of Dr. Balta by Dr. Kajic, at the time was there any explanation given about why this replacement was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, was there anything said about Dr. Kajic having military experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing was said. In respect of Dr. Kajic, we voted for Dr. Kajic. Several other physicians also were candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Dr. Balta in any way lacking in skills necessary at that stage to run the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the issue. I believe that he just -- his authority was being limited more and more, and I believe that that was the reason why he resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His authority was being limited by whom? The last question on that topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By Bruno Buzuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second question: The decision on who was to be released from the cinema on health grounds, did you make any of those decisions or were they made by others or by another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By others. That is, by one other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Franjo Tibolt, in cooperation with Stipo Krizanac. He was -- he stayed there to be in the position of decision making.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question from me, relating to the man Causevic who was complaining of what had been done to him by Cicin, what ultimately happened to Causevic; did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Causevic was killed in Old Vitez by a sniper bullet. It was a direct hit, and his heart was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness S, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the blinds are being --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the blinds are being brought down, the next witness is a substantial witness. I'm happy to say that a summary was available on Wednesday and was served on the Defence on that day, it being made clear that it was a draft document, and that further exhibits would be served as soon as they could be prepared. I think the exhibits were served on Friday. By my oversight, I didn't serve the draft summary on the Court, thinking that it might have been amended. It would have helped if I had done. I gather there are no or no substantial amendments to it, in any event. Can I make it available through the usual offices now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Half an hour. It will be 11.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I start the evidence of this witness, and get him to give us his name and so on, can the Court very kindly distribute to the members of the Chamber bundles of exhibits. Can the witness then have a bundle in front of him. There, I think, is one bundle left, which can be the Chamber's master bundle. The usher will discover that we are going to touch documents swiftly and briefly, getting the witness to deal with them from his seat. But it may be possible for the usher to put the relevant document on the overhead projector for the assistance of the public as we go along, but without taking time. The witness has, of course, spent time preparing to give evidence here in boiling down his material to the summary that you now have. He asked that he may have a copy of his outline before him, or summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've already had the advantage of some helpful indications from Mr. Sayers as to which paragraphs in the summary are paragraphs he would prefer me not to lead and to have dealt with in the conventional way. And I think I've got enough to get me up to lunch. And I'll, I hope, manage to conclude marking my paragraphs in accordance with Mr. Sayers' instructions after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness give us please his first name?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: My name is Hendrik Morsink.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A Dutch army officer since 1976, presently a Colonel? Just say "yes" if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And a monitor with ECMM from the 13th of April until the 13th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Arriving in Zenica on the 16th of April, 1993, was there a considerable amount of small arms fire observed by you coming from Serbian forces on the road from Visoko to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, after being briefed that fighting was going on over all the borders of the Vance-Owen Plan, did you, along with other monitors, Friis-Pederson and Lausten, go to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that road to Vitez, did you see -- and close to Nadioci and Pirici -- did you see six bodies, dead bodies, on the road?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were you informed about those bodies, so far as their previous movement of the bodies is concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was told by one of the monitors in the same car that he felt this very strange because he was told that BritBat had removed bodies from the road the night or the evening before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so they had been put back on the roadside?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you informed where they had been moved on the previous day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. As I recall it, they were moved to the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then put simply back on the road itself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also see houses that had been destroyed still smoking as a result of fire?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall there were a lot of houses alongside the road still smoking or still on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you introduced in Vitez to the Busovaca Joint Commission, being briefed on its background and structure by Remi Landry and Lausten, the ECMM monitor to whom I have referred?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your role at that time being to take notes and as a member of the team being sent out to carry out investigations and report back with your findings?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we are going to hear, you later on presided over that commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Throughout the events, of which you are going to tell us, were you assisted by interpreters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, we had several interpreters, Marijan and Milica, both being from Croat background, and several other interpreters from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have trouble ever with your chosen interpreters being accepted by the various parties to whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall only once in a small incident in Busovaca where one of my female interpreters, Milica, was rejected by the ABiH side, but Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic took immediate action and ordered the brigade commander to accept my interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever have any reason to doubt the accuracy of the translation done by your interpreters or the integrity with which they approached their work?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I had no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same 17th of April, did you meet the defendant, Mario Cerkez, in the HVO headquarters at the cinema in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By what title was he introduced to you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was introduced to me as a brigade commander of the brigade in Vitez, the HVO brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The name of that brigade being?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I can't recall that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if it's put in the summary and you want to turn to that, without objection, for assistance, you may.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I have got the summary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be preferable for you not to have to look at it, save when necessary.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The brigade is something like Stjepan, but I don't know the second name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stephan Masevic. Is that the name that you recall?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Putting that on one side so far as you can, how easy or difficult was it to get through to Cerkez's office?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that it was quite difficult because of fighting in the streets and because there were a lot of guards in front of the building and inside the building on all floors and nearly in front of every door. So it took us a long time to get to his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time, what was the level of conflict or fighting in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In Vitez itself, I recall there was still some small arms firing. Even the windows were hit several times during our first visit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, as you were informed and understood, was Cerkez's position in the hierarchy and area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was informed that he was the brigade commander of the Vitez Brigade. So I drew my conclusion that he was responsible for the vicinity and the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few documents. The first one, which is by this date slightly historic, Z607. You have the pack to your right. The usher needn't trouble with that at all. Usher, leave the documents for the witness. If the usher could have the other pack, please, then the witness can simply look at the documents and the usher can place the appropriate pages on the ELMO. And in that way we'll save time. So if the witness has his own pack. Thank you very much. This document pre-dates your arrival, because it's dated the 5th of April. It's a decision about the merging of HOS with units of the HVO. Was it an order with which you were familiar?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that I was informed about HOS and HVO during one of the first days of my stay in the area of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to this particular order, were you aware of its provisions or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was -- I don't recall that I saw this order myself, but I was informed of the contents of the order by Mr. Tibolt and by Mr. Remi Landry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, Z590, is a daily operational report. Before I turn to the contents of this report, inform the Chamber, please: Did you keep any contemporaneous records of your own?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote most of these daily operational orders myself. So I took copies of those daily orders. Sometimes I was asked to make a special report. I took copies of those as well. And I took notes during all the meetings I attended or during the meetings I chaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also make and do you retain any form of diary or personal diary that you'd been able to refer to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I used to write in my personal diary every night all the events that occurred during that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at this document, for the 17th of April, at the end of the first paragraph, 1(a), sets out the visits to Mario Cerkez. And in paragraph (b) does it read as follows: "In Vitez there is an almost full war going on." I must pause. I trust the interpreters have been provided with packs? And although I am listening in English, if I go too fast in any reading, I hope somebody will inform me so that I can slow down. "In Vitez there is an almost full war going on. Shelling and SA firings have been heard during the whole day." SA meaning?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Small arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Mortars and trenches are located very close to BritBat camp (to get cover?). At 1650 HVO are trying to force the Muslim people near --" Can you interpret the next word for me?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The BCJ house. That's the Busovaca Joint Commission house. In fact, the ECMM house near to the British Battalion camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "And the houses used by BritBat in the area. A very unpleasant situation. British officers and ECMM took immediate action to prevent this and made clear to all parties that people were to stay in their own houses and that BritBat would patrol the area close by the BritBat camp during night to prevent any attacks." Yes. The mortars and trenches that you refer to in the second line of paragraph (b), whose arms were those or whose positions were those?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You can't say that in common whose they were. There were several heavy artillery positions controlled by the HVO on the mountain called Mosunj. That was approximately one kilometre south of the British camp. And there was a hill on the other side of the camp, I think it's called the Grbavica hill, and this hill was controlled by the army of BiH. So they had artillery or mortars. I think the HVO had most of the artillery and mortars were most of the time used by the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this meeting, although it may not say it here, did you see anything of any other leading officials? Over the page, please, to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You mean during the same meeting with Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that Mr. Valenta, Anto Valenta, joined the meeting. I think approximately halfway through the meeting he entered the room and joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn now from whatever method of recollection is appropriate, your notes or this note, or memory, to what was said. Can you help us, please, with what the position of the Busovaca Joint Commission was? What was it aiming to do?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The Busovaca Joint Commission was raised early in '93, when a conflict started in the area of Busovaca, and the ECMM took the initiative to try to get both parties on the table again and to negotiate and to establish a ceasefire. And when new fightings occurred in April 1993, ECMM more or less picked up the work of the Busovaca Joint Commission again and tried to set an example in the area of Vitez, as well as was done in Busovaca. So that's the reason why it was still called the Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the attitude adopted on this day, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
