utterances.text: I'm not sure whether they already took the initiative the day before, but I was informed on the 17th that this was the nature of the Busovaca Joint Commission, as we explained to Mr. Cerkez, what the nature of our visit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His reaction?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I have to look in one of my notebooks, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's been summarised in the summary, and subject to objection, it may be you can look to that as a quicker route; being able to go back to your notebook, if issues are challenged.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The discussion was about the conflict, who started what, some historical background, and I recall that we asked or Friis-Pederson and I asked Mr. Cerkez if we could stop the fighting. And he replied saying that foreign forces from Zenica had to be stopped first. Until that he couldn't stop fighting in his area of responsibility. And he also told us that a lot of his soldiers were out of control. And I remember that I objected against this, because soldiers out of control cannot properly operate with artillery pieces. You need good maps for that. You need good communications to properly use artillery. So it cannot be done by soldiers out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The foreign forces in the other side, how did he describe them?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He referred to the forces on the other side as Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What at that stage was your awareness of the presence of foreign forces, Mujahedin or otherwise, assisting the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall that I was aware about Mujahedins on the 17th, my first day. I recall that I was informed about Mujahedins later on, but they always were mentioned about small groups of individuals. And there was one unit in Zenica called the 7th Muslim brigade, and this unit was told to be part of this Mujahedin group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the evidence, as you ever found it, to be of the number of Mujahedin, if any, taking part in either that brigade or any other?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The only exact number I ever found evidence of was the exchange of prisoners later on, and that was dealing with 11 foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I'm going back to the question or, rather, the answer where Mr. Cerkez, to the Colonel, he said that there were very many soldiers whom he could not control any longer, and the witness objected to this, speaking about artillery operations which needed a logistic back-up and which could not be done by soldiers who were not controlled by Mr. Cerkez. Could we hear now if Mr. Cerkez responded to this objection or not, and how did he react when the witness commented that he could not have a larger number of soldiers outside his control? Did he answer to that, and what did he answer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do not recall a direct answer to that, since Mr. Friis-Pedersen was the one to do most of the talking; I was the one to take notes. As I recall, the conversation just went on and they didn't mention this item anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had Mr. Cerkez given detail, given chapter and verse, of how, contrary to your proposition, troops were able to be out of control? Is that something you would have noted, do you think?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think so, yes, because my first reaction would have been, "If you are a brigade commander responsible for a certain area, then you should try to take control over all your soldiers and not just a few groups of these soldiers." There's only one commander responsible in his area of operation, his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Still part of paragraph 10, the 7th Muslim Brigade, did that ever appear in local structures of the military?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I only recall that the 7th Muslim Brigade was stationed in Zenica, and I never heard of any signs or allegations or rumours that this brigade, as a unit, was at the front line anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up the point that Judge Bennouna has raised about troops allegedly being out of control, in relation to the 7th Muslim Brigade, were you ever told by Merdan something about them being out of control?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Because there were a lot of complaints about Mujahedins, we referred to Merdan several times about this and asked him how this could be, and I recall that after a while -- I'm not sure when, but I think it's maybe the first or the second week of May -- he informed us that this 7th Muslim Brigade was under control now. So it took him some time, but as I recall, it was the first or the second week of May until this unit was under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We must now come back then, having dealt with that topic, but stick with the same meeting of the 17th. Were you told something about the taking of prisoners by the HVO in the course of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. We raised that item ourselves, and we were informed by Mr. Cerkez that he had several people taken in prison, most of them male. He already released the women and children, he told us. I don't recall the exact number, but it was something under a hundred. He considered every male in the area as somebody able to fight, and that's the reason why he brought them into prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he raise any other argument for the detention of these people?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Sometimes the argument of the personal safety was mentioned. So for the safety of these people themselves, they used to take them into prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anto Valenta, whom you told us joined the meeting, what views did he express?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that he was -- he used a lot of time to teach us about history, and after a while he told us that this whole fight was organised by the ABiH side and that the Muslims caused the problems themselves, and he appeared to be quite a hardliner in his thinking, in his political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've dealt with paragraph 13. Without looking at the summary, please, could you just cast your mind back not just to this meeting but to the developing history in the region? First of all, at this meeting, the involvement of people not in military uniform, if Valenta was not in military uniform, how did that strike you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was actually wearing a uniform, and that, in fact, struck me because I never saw politicians wearing uniforms, and he introduced himself as the vice-president of the HDZ. So he introduced himself as a politician, but the fact that he was wearing a uniform and had free access to the office of the brigade commander, that struck me, that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say he had free access, just enlarge on that, again not necessarily restricted to this meeting but to the overall period of time.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, it took us always quite some effort to get up to the brigade commander or sometimes even to the operational zone commander, and, well, it surprised me that these political people had no problems entering meetings where we were present, had no problems entering headquarters, and they sometimes even took an active part in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're going to be telling us a little bit more about things in detail over the forthcoming weeks, but in summary, how did military personnel on both sides of the conflict show their desire to cooperate or not in achieving solutions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Depending on the situation, sometimes they were very willing to cooperate, sometimes less willing. But in common, they were willing to cooperate, and they assigned liaison officers to our work, and they were of great help, these liaison officers. After a while, specifically the politicians showed up to be hardliners in thinking, and they sometimes refused to work with us, or sometimes they tried to take a lot of time by speaking about history again and again, and stating that, in fact, they should be the ones to talk with and not the officers in charge. After a while, they even tried to take over the work of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see, from the way your first couple of reports are prepared, that ceasefires were a central object of the work you were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The military leaders, when they had control, were there prospects of ceasefires?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: After a while, I think there were real prospects, since they agreed in freedom of movement for us after a few days; they agreed in joining us in meetings in a neutral place, the ECMM house; they agreed in being escorted from one place to another; so they felt safe, more or less, and the liaison officers from both sides went to every occasion where we had to check on allegations. So I think they were cooperative and they more or less believed in a ceasefire, although they misused every occasion to gain some benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time the politicians had taken greater control, what had happened to the prospects of ceasefires?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As I recall it, I didn't really like the politicians to mix in with our work, because since they did, the soldiers were no longer willing to cooperate and ceasefires were more often broken. The freedom of movement gave us more and more problems because roads were blocked, sometimes by civilians, and soldiers then used to say that they couldn't break these roadblocks because they were built up by civilians and politicians refused to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One matter of detail on the same topic. The man Valenta, did he, in due course, assume a position in relation to the prison commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What position was that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He informed me that he was assigned as the head of the commission of prisoners, whatever that might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you date that, approximately, or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think it was on the first or the second day when I met him, so the 17th or the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that job was later taken over by someone else.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A politician?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Mr. Skopljak took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning from that longer view to the meeting itself and then to the day of the 17th of April, did you, on that same day, attempt to get to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. We desperately tried to go to Kruscica, since there was the other side in this conflict. This village of Kruscica was controlled by part of the ABiH Brigade, and we had to reach this brigade commander to establish a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: But we did not manage to get into Kruscica, since the road was blocked by mines and soldiers and they told us that it wasn't safe for us to go there, so we were not allowed to use the road and we couldn't go to Kruscica that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, towards the back of your packs of exhibits, there are the maps and photographs. If the Chamber needs to remind itself of locations, there's an extract from the map marked 2175, and that, if the usher would like to have it at hand, it can always be laid on the ELMO when we are speaking about places such as Kruscica, which is shown conveniently immediately south of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can see the photographs, but I can't see a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I hope it's just before the photographs in the pile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, not in mine, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be the Chamber, for the time being, can remember the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The usher has managed to place one on the ELMO, so the Chamber can always refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your return, Colonel, on that day to the ECMM house, did you see something of activity at some houses around the BritBat base?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. There was one concrete road adjacent to the BritBat base, and at this road there was our ECMM house borrowed from a Croat lady. At this road, there were seven or eight more houses, most of them occupied or owned by Muslims, and a Croat force of approximately actually 10 or 15 men, led by an officer, tried to force these Muslim people out of their houses and tried to make them leave the houses and move away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The resolution of that was by whom?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: By the British 2IC of the battalion. I think it was Major Watters. He led quite a large group of British soldiers, and he made a firm protest against this HVO officer, that these houses were used by British officers and that these people -- these Muslim owners of the houses should stay in their own houses, and that ethnical cleansing was not allowed or not accepted by BritBat in the vicinity of the British Battalion camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document in the bundle is also dated the 17th of April. It's an exhibit already tendered as 696. It's over the three names with a common, it would appear to the untutored eye, a common signature, the three names, Puljic, Kostroman and Kordic, and it's a document that begs all possible protection for the Croats at Zenica and so on. Were you acquainted -- did you see this exhibit at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I didn't get it myself, but it was discussed by Mr. Thebault and by Colonel Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the significance of its contents being?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, they informed me about the concern of Croats, and about the allegations that Croats in Zenica were threatened by Mujahedins, and that their lives were apparently in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to verify or were the other monitors able to verify the accuracy of the information or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We called the regional centre in Zenica about this, and Mr. Thebault had already got a copy of this, and I recall that he denied this and that he would investigate the situation of all Croats in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was information forthcoming to support this document or was this incorrect, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You mean a protest like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There were more protests made like this, most of them oral and sometimes written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Supported by evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, they were never supported by evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We turn to the 18th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, this document, could we learn from the witness who signed the document, because we see the same signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe the witness won't know, but we'll see if he can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you able to help at all, from your knowledge, either, one, do you recognise any of these initials or signatures or, two, was this form whereby names would appear with common signatures something that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I don't recall these signatures, and I can't tell you who signed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. Nice, perhaps you should try and find another way to authenticate these signatures, because we see names, we see the title, "Vice-President of HZ-HB", Mr. Dario Kordic, the Secretary General, Mr. Kostroman, Mr. Puljic, but we see the same signature on top of all three names. We should know who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Suffice to say, but, of course, the authorship of documents coming from this body are known to that body rather than to us. This document is received by BritBat and made available to this Tribunal. It's not challenged, I think, that it comes with the apparent authority of those whose names appear, and it's something for others to answer, not for us, how it comes that they have three identical signatures. But the authority of the document is not, I think, challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to the 18th of April, paragraph 17? On that day, was there a meeting of the Busovaca joint commission at the ECMM house in Bila --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- to arrange a ceasefire, to list the missing and the dead, to deal with the exchange of prisoners, to investigate murders and other atrocities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO representative being Borislav Jozic and the Muslim representative from 325 Mountain Brigade being Rifet Hajdarevic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following that meeting, did you go to the headquarters of the HVO in Vitez, and did you see the defendant Cerkez there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We asked him about a letter of authorisation for his liaison officer so he could be of any help during our efforts to go to the other side, to Kruscica, to break checkpoints and roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything himself about what had been happening elsewhere in Zenica and so on?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, we asked them again about the conflicts, why he couldn't stop the fighting, and he kept complaining about the Croats, like stated in the former -- in the letter you showed me. He complains that the Croats in Zenica were unsafe and that we had to do something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he make any specific -- it's in the summary and it's not challenged, I think, about murders in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There were a lot of complaints, allegations about atrocities of Croats in Zenica, atrocities supposedly done by Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Cerkez at some stage in a state of some excitement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was quite upset, yes. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did he calm down?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, as we gave him some time to inform us about his concerns. And when we tried to inform him that according to our acknowledgement the Croats in Zenica were safe, then he calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His attitude towards removing roadblocks being what?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was still not very willing to give us freedom of movement. But after we insisted on that, he told the liaison officer to organise the safe passage of lines for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then attempt to go to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, on the 18th. That was the first time that we managed to go to Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get there and find some Croat prisoners being detained there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. We first met the commander on scene from the ABiH side, Mr. Sifet Sivro, and he informed us that he had a few prisoners as well. And we were able to visit these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Their condition? Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They were kept in a shed near a school. And the condition of one man was -- I think he was ill, mentally ill and physically ill. And the condition of the others was as such not bad, but it was not a place to keep people in a shed like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there complaints made by the HVO about the presence of outside troops fighting in the area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that these complaints were made several times, that units from Zenica sometimes referred to as Mujahedins, other times just as foreign units, were threatening the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to find any evidence of that yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: At that time we were not able to visit the front line along the Kuber hills -- those are the hills between Zenica and Vitez -- because there was still fighting going on. But we asked the other side, and they said that just this Mountain Brigade, I think it's 321st Mountain Brigade, that this was the only brigade that was fighting in the area. But I was not able to check myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return to HQ and did you raise the issue of roadblocks and of fighting near the BritBat base, and to that did the defendant Cerkez raise again the issues of alleged massacres in Zenica and of involvement by Mujahedins and of an alleged massacre in Kuber?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he blame the ABiH for the starting of the fighting in Bila at the BritBat base and claim that three HVO soldiers had been shot near that base?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. This appeared to be the common way of working, complaining and then -- because of these complaints, finding an excuse for your own behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he demand the cessation of massacres by the ABiH and require them to treat people properly?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he asked us to investigate this and to organise that the Croats in Zenica were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he say would happen if they were shot at again; they, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that he said that he would -- his soldiers would return fire as soon as they were shot at, and that if Croats were not safe, that he would organise things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say what, if anything, would happen to houses if they were shot at?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If they were shot at from certain houses, then they would burn them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His allegations of massacres in Zenica and Kuber, were they capable of verification?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The allegations in Zenica were verified the same night by monitors in Zenica. And the Kuber area was escorted by BritBat, I think, two or three days later, to check on these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say they were verified, do you mean they were verified, the allegations, and found to be true?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Found to be untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Found to be untrue. In both cases?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In both cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The effect of this information on these complaints by the HVO was what, so far as Croats living in the area was concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The effect on the Croat population was that they were very scared and they were in fear; that similar things as these allegations that supposedly were done to the Croats in Zenica should happen or would happen to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any of these Croats living away from their own houses, but with the prospect of returning to their own houses?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There was an area northwest of Zenica that I visited in the second week of my period in middle Bosnia, and there happened more or less the same: Croats were very scared, fled to a small village called Grahovici. Some 2.000 or 3.000 Croats went there. And with the help of Croat police from Zenica, I managed to convince the people that it was safe to go back to their own houses. But the day, then, when we arrived with buses to bring the people back, they were told by Croats, officers and by Croat politicians, that it was no longer safe for them to stay in the area of Zenica and they should go to a safe place, Vitez or Nova Bila. So they were informed by their own politicians and soldiers not to come with us to Zenica, not to trust us, but to go to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this same day, did you go to Rovna?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And perhaps the usher would very kindly put it on the ELMO, in case the Chamber hasn't got maps. I'll deal with any deficiency of maps at the short adjournment. But Rovna is southeast of Vitez and about ten centimetres or a couple of inches, two or three inches southeast. From Rovna were you able to hear and see something happening in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. From Rovna, that's approximately three kilometres from Vitez, when we visited the ABiH front line site in Rovna, we heard several explosions on the hill side of Kuber. That's northeast of Vitez. And then one large explosion and a big pile of smoke and dust in the direction of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently discover what it was that had exploded?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to go there the same afternoon, but the road was blocked. And when we arrived in the British camp, we were informed that a large truck bomb had been exploded in the outskirts of Stari Vitez. And the day after we visited that spot ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn from the 18th of April, there are two documents in the stack. Take them slightly out of order. The second one first, Z718, a document already exhibited. This is your report for the day itself, the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, this is my daily report. It says on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we can see common patterns in the preparation of these reports. I needn't go through everything. But we can see at the foot of the page under "other," it sets out your meetings with Mr. Cerkez and sets out the various things that he said there. And then over the page at subparagraph headed "e" is the conclusion about the attempt from the HVO side of yesterday evening to make ethnic cleansing in the village of -- in the village Bila close to BritBat failed, and then you set out why. Thank you. Exhibit Z708 of the same day, also already tendered, coming from the HVO, going to UNPROFOR, being a protest, alleges that in the severe attacks on Croatian villages of Zenica municipality, Muslim forces are using all their bestiality and cruelty, as well as their evident wish of destroying all that is Croatian. And then says in the next paragraph, "The arrested men were thrown under tanks." This particular protest, was it one you saw at the time or not, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I can't recall that I saw it myself. I don't recall that I have a copy of this, and most of the times I took copies myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this particular form of protest familiar or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's very familiar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And such allegations as men being thrown under tanks, to your knowledge ever sustained evidently?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, never sustained. I wasn't even aware of ABiH having tanks. Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, will you just give me one minute while I check something. Paragraph 23 -- sorry, 22. On the 19th of April did the Busovaca Joint Commission meet again in the same ECMM building; did Jozic compile a list of 70 prisoners saying there may be more in the region; and did the Muslim representative, Hazdarevic, indicate that he had problems getting organised because he was unable to get through to his headquarters in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following that meeting, did you go and meet Cerkez and Valenta again in Vitez at the HQ and the cinema?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they promise that roadblocks would pose no more problems for your commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ask them about the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Valenta's explanation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: At first he tried to find an explanation like a house was set on fire near an ammunition storage site, and then they said that the storage side might have been hit by a mortar shell. And then later on they said that the Muslim side caused this explosion themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who gave the explanation about spreading fire? Can you remember? If necessary, you can check your notes, but if you can remember, so much the quicker.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's in my notes. I'm not sure who said what.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find any of these explanations acceptable?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I did not, because this large truck bomb exploded very close to the mosque of Stari Vitez, and it appeared to be a clear threat to the Muslim inhabitants of that area of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it appear, in your experience as a soldier, to have military justification?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, not at all. It's never allowed to use means like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The note of who said what, was that note originally made the same day or thereabouts? Who gave what explanation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The notes in my small notebook were made by myself during the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this occasion, I think we better hear what it was that Cerkez gave -- Mr. Cerkez gave as an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just intrude. We have made a generic request for notes that are to be used by witnesses to refresh their recollection during testimony. We have not been provided with a copy of Colonel Morsink's notes. I do not know what the Chamber's attitude towards that is, but obviously I would assume, anyway, that they are written in Dutch, and translation problems being what they are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are written in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Written in English. Well, if we could have a copy of them, perhaps over the break, that would be extremely helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any difficulty about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that the Chamber's policy has been that if documents aren't handled and seen by us, but are simply referred to by the witness, it's the witness's response that may matter. I suspect that this witness won't have any objection. He can just be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't seen that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've seen them in the sense that we've been with him when he's been referring to them, but we haven't had them ourselves, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't got copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't got copies ourselves, I don't think, no. And I think -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Normally the Defence counsel, I think, are entitled to see documents which are referred to refresh memories, provided there is no particular objection from the witness. I'll ask the Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No objection. Perhaps you could show it or the relevant parts to the Colonel during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I can put it on the ELMO if you like. I can put it on the ELMO and read it. The markings are made later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the explanation by Cerkez, just read it out and interpret it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: "The explosion came from a house. Later info was that the truck exploded. There is no exact info on what happened." And then Eric Friis-Pederson said, "Please investigate this. This is terrorism. It is not fair."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Cerkez's response to the request to investigate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I wrote down and underscored that Mario will investigate. So Mr. Cerkez told us that he would investigate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this within his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It was clearly within the vicinity of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again on -- in your experience as a soldier, on whom would have fallen the responsibility of a -- investigating a matter of this sort at that time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: According to my acknowledge, it is the area of responsibility of the brigade commander on scene, and this was clearly within the area of responsibility, and every action like this or incident like this should be investigated by or by somebody under the command of the brigade commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was any investigation by Cerkez carried out?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any more of this inquiry after this day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. I recall that we asked about it, but there was no investigation made or, at least, we didn't get any results of any investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Towards the back of the -- in fact, right at the back of the bundle of exhibits there is an Exhibit Z2534, which is a selection of photographs taken by the witness with his own handwritten captions on them. If we turn on a few sheets, three sheets I think, we see something of the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if you'd like to ensure that -- that's it. Can you just tell us when you took these photographs and what they reveal?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I told you we were not able to go to Old Vitez, to Stari Vitez that same day on the 18th. But as I recall it, we were able to use this very road on the 19th, and you can clearly see the bodies still hanging out of the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just point that out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: [Indicating] And I was informed by the British Battalion that they already evacuated all wounded people and homeless people, and they had problems removing the dead bodies because of danger of the house collapsing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the bottom of the three photographs on this sheet, were you able to identify where the truck bomb had been at the time of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, you can still see a crater in the middle of the road and the dark part on top of that. That is the remains of the truck. I think it's the engine, the gearbox.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The mosque to which you referred, it may not be shown precisely here, I'm not sure, but can you give us a --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that the mosque is on this side where the grass is and the small fence. I'm not sure from what side we came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To orientate ourselves, and only if you can remember, keeping the bottom picture in mind, if the usher can now just show the top picture. They won't all fit on the ELMO together. But the top picture, where is that in relation to the truck bomb and the view from the bottom picture?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's very, very close to the location where the bomb exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if it's on the left-hand side of the road or the right? It doesn't matter, probably.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you. Turning to your discussions with Cerkez and Valenta, paragraph 24. Was a claim made about what the ABiH was doing in relation to BritBat base?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that we made a protest, and also BritBat made a protest in the direction of the HVO, a protest for these attempts of removing the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was Cerkez's attitude to that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: His reaction, as I recall it, was that the ABiH was using BritBat as a kind of a place to take shelter behind. So they, according to Mr. Cerkez, they used the BritBat to hide their mortar positions and to move troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did Valenta say about things, and in particular what did he say about any ceasefire order he had received?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't exactly recall what he replied to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll read it from the summary and you can be corrected if it's necessary. Did he assert that the HVO had received a ceasefire order and asked whether the ABiH had received it as well?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He is referring to the meeting of the day before, where we -- where both sides agreed in a ceasefire, and he was more or less checking on it, whether the other side was living up to this ceasefire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you visit some prisoners in cellars -- in a cellar controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see some prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that we -- I think it was in the cellar of the cinema, so that's the brigade headquarters in Vitez, where we saw approximately 70 male prisoners all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did they appear to you to being treated?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They appeared to be treated quite well. They told us through the interpreter that they were fed well and that they could use the toilet, if needed; that they got some signs of contact from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Did you then go to Kruscica and meet Sifet Sivro, commander for that area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he prepared, representing the ABiH, to accept a ceasefire, notwithstanding the truck bomb, which, of course, caused -- it says "upset" here, but maybe rather more than upset.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. He was very upset, but he still accepted the ceasefire, as agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he assert that he'd given orders that prisoners kept by his side should be well treated?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did he confirm that Hajdarevic on his side, and Jozic on the HVO side, could talk in order to create a weapons-free zone around the BritBat camp?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 20th of April, paragraph 26: Meeting of the BJC concerned with prisoner exchange and the need for accurate lists, and for the evacuation of the wounded. Was there heavy artillery and mortar fire that morning?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, there was a lot of artillery fire going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming from whose positions, as you could judge?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The positions we could clearly see were these Mosul positions I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Occupied by?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Occupied by HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you learn about an ultimatum to inhabitants of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that, in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We were told that the inhabitants of Gacice were ordered to leave their houses and to go to Zenica, and they were threatened by local soldiers or by local civilians or both, and the set-up was to try to scare these people away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document, Z754, already tendered. Paragraph 3, "ceasefire violations (unconfirmed)." "Tanks were told to be in position on the mountain road between Zenica and Vitez. Shelling HVO headquarters and the PTT building in Vitez. HVO is said to be putting an ultimatum on Gacice and that failed. HVO is said to have started attacking this village." Were the HVO complaints, as recorded here, true or unconfirmed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We didn't find any signs of any tanks used by the ABiH side, nor of any tanks in position on the mountain road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 28, the 21st of April. On that day, at the BJC, was there a meeting between Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, the deputy commander for the operational zone for Central Bosnia, Franjo Nakic for the HVO, Dzemal Merdan, the local commander for the 3rd BiH Army, also being present. And was it at this meeting that a decision was made to form local joint commissions, LJC's as we called them, in Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik and Busovaca, with a joint command in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the representatives of both sides in Vitez agree to have direct communication between themselves, even if the whole of the commission was not constituted or present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that same 21st, did you visit Ahmici for the first time, discovering one body, an elderly man, in a garage?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 30, but don't refer to the summary and just help us from your memory. On this occasion, on this day, did you meet a man called Father Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I was asked to escort Father Stjepan from Zenica to Vitez, since he wished to visit his colleague Catholic priests in Vitez and to inform them about the situation in Zenica and to be informed himself about the situation in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you meet somebody else there in the presence of Father Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I met the Catholic priests in Vitez. I don't remember the names, but there were two young priests. During this meeting, Pero Skopljak entered the house near the church where we had the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you met him before or was this the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I never met him before. This was the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His attitude?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He also started speaking about the history and the background of this whole conflict. Since he found out that I -- that my German is not too bad, he started speaking in German to me, and I found out he was really very hard in his conclusions and in his ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His attitude towards the United Nations and also his attitude towards Muslims, please?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: His attitude towards the United Nations was very negative. He complained that the BritBat didn't do anything to help Croat victims in the car bomb incident, although to my knowledge there were no Croat injuries. He said that the U.N. was no longer impartial, that his people could not trust the U.N. anymore, and his attitude towards Muslims was very, very negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you recall his saying about Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that he stated that Muslims had caused this conflict themselves and they had brought this curse on their own back, that they were the ones to be blamed for all the victims in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Father Stjepan, on the other hand, how did you find him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was very moderate. He had a clear view of the whole situation. He tried to calm down his colleague priests and tried to calm down Mr. Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By my oversight, I turned to the 22nd of April without dealing with the document that touches the 21st of April, which we'll produce very briefly. It's the next in the stack, Z771. Probably the second page is worth noting at subparagraph D. It deals with your findings in Ahmici, and I'm not going to go into it in any detail. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry for taking that out of order. Back to the summary, paragraph 31, and on to the 23rd of April, a meeting at Vitez of the local joint commission, with little progress being made, although there were promises to switch on the telephone switching stations of the PTT, both of which were controlled by the HVO. Were the telephone systems, to your knowledge, damaged by consequences of fighting or were they just switched off?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think they were not damaged at all. Maybe a single line was damaged. But the stations, as such, were fully operational or capable of operating, but they were merely switched off, and not all the lines. Some lines were switched off and some others were not, since the headquarters of the HVO Brigade and the operational zone in Vitez were still able to call BritBat on the special PTT line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So Z793, the next document, again we deal with it briefly. Subparagraph 4 on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- records that this was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a small technical question. So far, a couple of "Z" documents are introduced, but I'm not aware of whether they are taken as evidence material or just shown to the -- we never really produced those documents as being taken in the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I understood they were being produced as exhibits in the case, and some of them have already been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's certainly my intention that they should be produced, and indeed I thought that the ECMM documents generally are documents that both sides are going to regard as helpful when they are produced. But I needn't go through them in detail when the witness has given his evidence which is otherwise summarised and noted there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just afraid of technical problems, and recently the Chamber did give some instructions on that matter, in the sense that a document which is introduced should be clearly declared as introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, for my part, I understood that matters were being introduced as evidence, that any document put in is an exhibit unless somebody says something to the contrary. So if you've got any objection to any of these documents, say so. Otherwise, you must take them as exhibits. They've got numbers on them, and in order to save time, documents will be admitted unless there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's fine with me. That's okay, Your Honour. I just wanted to know whether each document which is presented is formally entered as the evidence. If so, I have no objection on any particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Unless there's an objection, documents tendered will be admitted. That will go for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Z7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just ten seconds, Mr. President. We have no objection, obviously, to the European Community Monitoring Mission documents being admitted as evidence provided they are all admitted. We object to selective documents being extracted by the Prosecution and selectively introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, because we don't have access to all of them, and that's a real problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a matter which we've discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it is. I think the representation was made or the point was made that there is no general library of these documents, but there appears to be quite an extensive source of supply of them, and we would just like to see them all to make sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution are entitled to select what they want and not produce everything. Obviously, they are producing a case, or presenting it. If there are other such documents, I would anticipate that normally they would be disclosed, unless there's some good reason to stop it. Mr. Nice, while we're dealing with this topic, we have discussed it before and I forgot what the result was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we discussed it twice. Once, at the end of a period before the summer recess, we discussed libraries of documents in general, and you expressed or perhaps hinted that it might be a good idea to be generous with this type of document, insofar as generosity lay within our gift. As to ECMM documents, however, they are not within our gift to make available, and I think I've explained before that the custodians of ECMM documents are prepared for us to produce them on this basis through the witnesses as relevant but would otherwise wish to be heard before any question of wholesale distribution is dealt with. It may be that that matter will have to come before the Chamber at some stage, because the Defence, as I understand it, have communicated directly with the holders of all the ECMM documents, requesting access to all the documents, so the matter will have to be litigated. I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's not go on with this. For the moment, we've got the witness here. These documents are admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm then on Z793, paragraph 4: "Tripartite Meetings." "During the first part of the JOC meeting, there was an exchange of ceasefire protests. The incident at the gas factory, Bilalovac, was discussed, and the ECMM representatives made a strong verbal protest. The allegation about eight Muslim villages northwest of Kiseljak was noted and during the meeting confirmed by a specialist British patrol. It was then agreed fulfilling the re-establishment of PTT lines. In Travnik, at the PTT building, a repair team was formed. The team managed to repair various items at two sites, but did not reconnect the communications as wished." Comments on that? Accuracy of complaints?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The complaints were made every meeting from both sides, complaints about breaking the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The PTT building and the repair team and so on?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We visited the director of the PTT in Travnik, and he sent a mechanic with us to Nova Bila and somewhere in Travnik -- I'm not sure where it was, but I'm very positive about Nova Bila -- and it was merely a matter of switching on the letters entered. I personally entered this switching station, and there was no damage visible. It was just a matter of putting on some switches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Over the page, please, to subparagraph 7(B) in the middle of the page: "The liaison officer from Canadian Battalion paid us a visit. It was then confirmed that the following Muslim villages had been burned down: Svinjarevo, Gomionica, Gromiljak, Polje Visnjica, Palez and Rotilj. The other reported alleged burned villages on the last report have not yet been confirmed. It appeared that those burned villages were set on fire mainly by incendiary munitions fired from artillery pieces from Kiseljak, and heavy" -- is that "machine gun"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "atrocities, including rapes, were confirmed in the village of Rotilj. It was discussed that there are possibilities to receive escort support from Canadian Battalion." I think that speaks for itself, doesn't it, as an entry?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn, for a period of time, to paragraph 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be a convenient moment, then. Colonel, we are going to adjourn now. During this adjournment and any others there may be in your evidence, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes members of the Prosecution. Would you be back, please, at half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 32. Colonel, between the 23rd and the 26th of April, did you stay in Zenica and were you involved in resettlement of large groups of Croats who had come from four villages: Janjac, Stranjani, Konjevica and Susanj, northwest of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Staying in Zenica, you mean? I didn't go to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I am just saying: Did you between that period of time for some time stay in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Overnight I stayed in Zenica, but I travelled from Zenica to the area of the four towns you just called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Those Croats, did they say that their resettlement was out of fear?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They left their homes and their villages because they were afraid of attacks. Some of the houses were actually damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, indeed, at Grahovici was Father Stjepan the Catholic priest from Zenica working together with you and indeed with them?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the local HVO commander and his soldiers take a part?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the beginning they cooperated with us and agreed that Father Stjepan and ourself and a few representatives of the displaced persons could check on the villages and the houses. And later on they, in spite of this co-operation, they told the people to go to Vitez and to Nova Bila. So they didn't cooperate in that second half of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they also broadcast accounts of things that may have been happening?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't think that they themselves broadcast this. It was broadcast by Croats, I think from the area of Vitez or maybe another larger city in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these broadcasts accurate or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They were not accurate. They were, as I saw it, meant to bring fear into the people and to warn them from their point of view not to go back to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an incident of firing over people's heads?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The Croat soldiers, the HVO soldiers in Grahovici, supported by HVO policemen, impressed the people by firing over their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the accounts of soldiers, were they reinforced by the television and radio broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I didn't see the broadcasts myself. I was told by the people that they had information through television and radio that it was unsafe for them to go back to their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the upshot of that was that many people left Zenica to go to Vitez, but in due course did some 1.600 Croats return to their villages while the other half went to and stayed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. Approximately 3.000 refugees were gathered in Grahovici, and approximately half of them went back to their own houses and the others used the buses we brought to bring them to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, did you go to Kiseljak to investigate allegations of robbery, looting and murders?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While there, did you find some 6 to 9 male prisoners held by the HVO in Kiseljak barracks being admitted to by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. We asked them whether they had prisoners, and they admitted that there is 6 to 9, and to show us these people. But they were not free to check the whole prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like, please, to turn to your album of photographs. Not album; your collection of photographs, just to bring to life what you were telling us about. About four sheets in. Starting with a picture of the priests, a couple of priests, and nuns on the top. Can you just tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's a picture of the local priests and nuns in Brajkovici, close to Gajovici [phoen]. And the priest on the right, with his arm on one of the monitors, that's Father Stjepan, the priest from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The bottom picture of the three?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's part of the group of Croats coming from the area of Zenica. You see the ECMM truck there. One of the nurses, one of the doctors is working inside this building and tried to get the confidence of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next sheet, still on the 26th of April, as the note of your own reveals. The top picture.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That is part of the group of the people who wished to go back to their own houses, and they are waiting for the buses to bring them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the middle and bottom pictures, do they bear on the same issue?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, but that's already in the area north of Zenica, so in the area where these people used to live. So some of them get out of the bus there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I've dealt with the 27th of April. The HVO admitted to holding six to nine male prisoners, but did it turn out to be rather more than that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, in the beginning of May, a lot of prisoners were released, and I think up to 50 or 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also go to Rotilj village?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, because there were allegations that massacres had happened in Rotilj. I went there for an investigation and I wrote a special report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Summarising the effect of that report, was the whole village being used as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Rotilj is in a small valley. It can easily be sealed off, and I think approximately 500, 600 people were more or less detained there, or they were not free to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not on the map we were looking at before. The people who were there, did they make some claims about their treatment at night, in particular?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that they were scared by soldiers in the hillside around this small valley. They were threatened by these soldiers, most of the times drunken soldiers. Shots were fired during the night and, as I said, they were not free to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Deaths and destruction of houses, can you enumerate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: What I saw myself was in the entrance of the village, six or seven houses were burnt. And when I asked the local HVO commander about this, he told me that he received fire from one of those houses and that one of his soldiers was wounded during that action, and that he had to destroy these houses to be able to defend himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: People killed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think 8 or 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you said 6 in your summary. May that be right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I have to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you try to get into Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, on that same day, because all these allegations about other villages in the area of Kiseljak being destroyed. I tried with the escort of Canadian armoured personnel carrier to go into Gomionica, but we were stopped at the outskirts of the village. I could see houses in flames, in smoke. There were quite a lot of soldiers on the hillside in defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the 28th of April, please. On that day did you note some UNHCR trucks, and if so, how many, and where were they headed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was back in the ECMM house at the evening of the 28th, and I was informed by BritBat and UNHCR, by our own radio means, that a convoy of some 40 trucks had been stopped in Busovaca. And they asked us to check it out and, if possible, to free the truck drivers and the trucks and the cargo. So I informed Colonel Bob Stewart about this and he sent me -- he gave me -- well, "gave" is maybe the wrong word. He attached a warrior unit with me and asked me to have a look in Busovaca and try to free those trucks. It was in the beginning of the evening, I think, maybe 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening. We went there with the warriors, and at the factory in the -- at the entrance of Busovaca we actually saw the trucks. Soldiers were unloading the trucks. A lot of cargo was thrown on the ground and damaged. And I addressed to the local commander there and told him that UNHCR had freedom of movement and couldn't just be stopped, and that the cargo was not for the HVO, but meant for the warehouse in Zenica. And I told them to stop this and to reload the trucks and to give them back. He did not agree. He said he had orders to check all trucks. And after a long discussion and some telephone calls by this local commander, he finally agreed in giving back the trucks and the cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document number -- the next one, Z840, please, which relates to this day, this is, in fact, a document prepared by Jean-Pierre Thebault. Are you able to comment on this document and its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second sheet on it.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Second sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the bottom, under paragraph 3, there's a reference to the trucks?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown this document before, and the passage, the 40 truck units --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "before", you mean in the course of attending here to give evidence in a previous trial --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- or do you mean you were shown it at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I wasn't shown it at the time, but I supplied the Ambassador Thebault with this information. So it's, in fact, my information that he used to write his report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When it reads, "40 trucks, UNHCR convoy of food supplies, escorted by two Warriors, was hijacked on its way to Zenica, and the HVO forces responsible for this action claimed that they did not care of the orders of Colonel Blaskic and Brigadier Petkovic concerning the free movement, that they had strict orders from Mr. Kordic, official highest-level representative of HVO for Central Bosnia, to arrest this convoy and search it," where had that intelligence or information come from?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You mean this information on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I informed the ambassador on this. Part of the information, I guess, came from BritBat itself, since I didn't make the phone calls myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you provided this information to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was it accurate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, the company of Warriors is a little bit exaggerated. There were, in fact, six Warriors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The following day, the 30th of April, paragraph 38, the local joint commission meeting concluded that the target of the agreement had not been reached. The allegation, I think, went to Dubravica managed to get some 300 Muslims released and achieved similar success in Kruscica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but in Dubravica, some 300 were released. In Kruscica, there were only, I think, eight or ten men held in prison, so they were all released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Josip Bozic gave you a list of prisoners of the Viteska Brigade held in Dubravica, in the cinema; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. It's hard to check whether this list was exactly the number of people held in Dubravica. Representatives of the ICRC checked on the freeing of all these prisoners, so they were present and they were the ones to check lists and make up their own lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, was there a further prisoner exchange, Kiseljak and Klokoti?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did the ceasefire agreement appear to hold?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. There I was informed that there were actually far more than those eight prisoners in Kiseljak. Some, I think 54, were released from Kiseljak. On the other side, approximately as well, 50 prisoners were released in Klokoti.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, did you visit Jelinak and see one Croat house on fire, apparently hit by an anti-tank rocket?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the local ABiH commander claim that there was no fighting going on in that area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Strane, the HVO commander behaved how?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In Strane, I met a man in military clothes who called himself Marinac, and he told us that he was the local HVO commander. He had a group of civilians with him carrying shovels, and they had kind of a porch they set under a tree, a group of approximately 10 or 15 male civilians. We asked them what they were doing with the shovels, but we were not allowed to talk to these civilians. This Mr. Marinac, he became angry and told us that we had to stop fighting from the other side and that he wouldn't see us any longer, so we had to leave his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did these men appear to be doing, so far as you could gather?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, my -- as far as I understood it or I estimated the situation, was that these people had been digging trenches, or digging defensive positions, or holes, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 3rd of May, did the local joint commission meeting result in ABiH claims that the HVO was cheating with prisoner lists?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further complaining of ill treatment such as by trench digging?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Nakic's response that a lot of Croat houses had been damaged, and in a later meeting with Skopljak, as head of the local commission of prisoners, and of Santic, did you talk about prisoner release?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did both sides refuse to release prisoners, despite receiving an order to do so?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, they were willing to release. But later on, as the allegations of cheating started and when civilians like Skopljak mixed in, they refused to release any further because they stated or they said that in Zenica, there were far more prisoners and they were only willing to release on a balanced basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't able to make any progress, notwithstanding the arrival --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you fail to achieve further progress, notwithstanding the involvement of Colonels Stewart and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. We informed Colonel Stewart, and he told us that he would go to Blaskic and try to speed up the process of releasing prisoners, since that was agreed upon on the 29th of April, but they both failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 44. Still on the 4th of May, was the local joint commission visited by Spanish, French, and U.K. ambassadors?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO representative, Nakic, did he claim that there was problems with release arising from civil authorities' failure to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Merdan's attitude was what?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They both had the opportunity to explain what happened in the last few days or weeks, and Merdan was very upset about the whole situation. He explained to the ambassadors that fighting started in Ahmici or started with the incident of Ahmici, and that it spread out all over the Lasva Valley, and later on similar things happened in the area of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You make specific reference to Gacice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He explained to the ambassadors that these tactics of burning houses and tactics of fear and scaring people and killing them hadn't stopped so far, since the last information was information from the night before that even in Gacice, a small village near Vitez, the ethnical cleansing was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any allegation of where HVO ideas and authority were coming from, from what level?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: According to Mr. Merdan, these ideas came from the top political level, from Mr. Boban and Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To which the HVO replied in what way?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's not fully clear to me whether they actually listened to these orders from the top political level. More than once, local commanders told me that they had contradictory orders, so it's hard to say who the direct orders came from; not to say for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, did Colonel Blaskic issue a call for help, in which he said something of the suffering of the Croats in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. He issued, more than once, kind of calls for help like this one. It's like the allegations you showed this morning, the written allegations. The contents of it, it's the same. It's an allegation that Croats in Zenica have been maltreated and have been threatened and that we, the International Community, should do as much as we can to save these people and to bring them into safety in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the allegations investigated and found to be true or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. Again, we were stationed in Zenica, so we had freedom of movement there and we could check on these allegations every day, and we again told Mr. Blaskic that they were untrue and that we didn't find any proof for these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same day, did you go to Gacice and discover that families, Muslim families, had left the night before and gone to Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. We checked, because Mr. Merdan told this to the ambassadors, we checked Gacice the same day, and all Muslim inhabitants left Gacice, altogether some 200, and we were told through our interpreter that these people had been forced to leave Gacice in trucks and they had to step off the trucks on the mountain road to Zenica and walk the last part in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
