utterances.text: Another matter on the 4th of May that isn't in your summary. It's in the original chronology, and for some reason, it hasn't been incorporated. At the moment, I don't have a further copy of the special report as an exhibit, but perhaps the witness may be able to help us from his own notes and we can complete the position later. Did you, on the 4th of May, go to a school in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I can find the names, but it was a mother and her daughter, a Muslim mother. She used to live in Vitez or on the outskirts of Vitez, and she had found shelter in the school in Vitez. She had a few personal belongings with her, and she complains that even when the school director guaranteed her safety, she still didn't feel safe because during the night soldiers knocked on the windows and brought fear onto this mother and daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think something happened to the dog. If you can't remember it, perhaps we'll go on to another matter. We're going to have it in the report in due course. But did you bring this matter to the attention of anyone?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that I spoke to the liaison officer who was with me, Mr. Borislav Jozic. We spoke to Mr. Cerkez about this, and again he claimed that drunken soldiers were free to move in Vitez during the night and that normally soldiers had to stay in barracks, but that he couldn't control these elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the sensible thing, I'm grateful to Mr. Scott, is if we can put this exhibit on the ELMO briefly, it's only one sheet, and I'll have it copied later. It will become or it is number 882.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without reading it in full, that sets out, does it, the investigation that was carried out visiting the families. And then if we run down -- our eyes down the page, go towards the bottom of the document, you summarised it already. There was, I think, reference to the dog being killed towards the -- halfway down the present screen. And then at the bottom, three lines, four lines up from the bottom: "The brigade commander was aware of these extremists, and told that he was searching for them, and that he would take care of the safety and wellbeing of the family." Does that cover the position, Mr. Morsink?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on from the 4th of May to the 9th of May. Go on from the 4th of May to the 6th of May, paragraph 46. And we will now come to Exhibit 887.1, which the witness may care to look at and can go on the ELMO. Did you on this day, the 6th of May, go to the joint HVO and ABiH headquarters in Travnik where Merdan and Nakic were based at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Making initial arrangements or arrangements for initial meetings of the three local commissions in Busovaca, Vitez and Kiseljak, later going to Busovaca where you came under fire in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From where were you under fire?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: From the HVO controlled outskirts of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there mutual blame, each side blaming the other?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I was on my way to visit the local ABiH commander in Kacuni, but I wasn't in his area of control, so I don't think that I blamed the ABiH side for this, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the document that's on the ELMO at the moment, one of yours. Under paragraph 2, that sets out some of the history, but I think the material feature, we can probably go straight down to the bottom of the document, to just over halfway down, where in halfway through a paragraph the local school director took care of these families, but even in the school they were threatened again, and their houses burned or looted. The team informed UNHCR of this matter. The team asked the commander of the HVO brigade in Vitez about the incident at Gacice. All Muslim families seemed to be forced to leave the village at the 3rd of May in the evening. They were brought with cattle trucks to Dubravica and were told to go to Zenica on foot. The brigade commander accused extremists of this incident. So that brigade commander was whom?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That was Mr. Cerkez, since it was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 47. On the 8th of May, was there the first meeting of the local commission in Busovaca and the first meeting in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were old problems rehashed and were there reports of shelling from both Zenica and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, this was the normal start of every meeting. They started with old problems and accusing the other side of starting and breaking the ceasefire and shooting with all kinds of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could now play a tape I think you'll be able to help us with. It's Exhibit 2769, part 1. And while that's being processed or progressed, the Chamber and my friends may choose to look at the loose photographs at the end of the album where there are some stills, numbers 2529, 2531 and 2533.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't probably stop it early enough, and that's my fault. But we can see the man in the foreground shown in 2529 and, indeed, in 2531, was whom?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This was Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll put the stills on the ELMO. Thank you very much. They are already there. Anybody else you can identify for the assistance of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. The man in the middle is Mr. Nakic, Mr. Franjo Nakic from the HVO side. And the man on the left-hand side is Dzemal Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph, is there anybody there who can be easily identified?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. There is Mr. Cerkez again on the right-hand side, and on the opposite side of the table is the ABiH side. I think the left-hand with the cap on is the brigade commander in Preocica, Mr. Kelestura, and the man in the middle, I only know the first name is Sefkija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The third photograph, 2533?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, our HVO liaison officer, Mr. Borislav Jozic, and the man on the left-hand side, I don't know his name, but I think it's one of the battalion commanders of the HVO brigade in Vitez. And I remember this man very well, since he threatened me -- to kill me if I would come to a roadblock again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a threat yet to be made?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that in its time, but that's the man?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You described him as a red-faced man from time to time. It's not quite so clear from the video reproduction. Paragraph 48. Did the mayor of Vitez, Santic, press a need for houses?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that he explained to me why a lot of Muslims had to leave their houses. He said, "We need the houses very urgently, since a lot of Croat refugees or DPs come from [indiscernible] territory and come from Muslim-held territory," so they urgently needed all these houses to house the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 49. On the 9th of May, with Lausten and doctors from Medicin du Monde, did you go to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time was it surrounded by the HVO, but did the ceasefire seem to hold?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you secure the removal or escape or exchange of two people?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Two people were ill, had to be treated in hospital. So we agreed in evacuating these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go on to Kruscica, where there was small arms firing, sniping and anti-tank rounds fired at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Muslim families there ask you to take out five Croat families, amongst them an old man who appeared to be badly beaten?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did other Croat families elect to stay behind?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you check or were you informed whether they had fear of the Muslim majority in the area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The people who asked to leave, they had fear. And the others who decided to stay, I checked them myself through my interpreter, of course, and I already had spoken to these families more than once, and they decided to stay, since they had their houses and their cattle there, and they did not experience as much fear as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the return to Vitez, did you see civilian trench diggers?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stop and see in a handheld video two bodies of ABiH soldiers allegedly killed or found dead in Vranjska?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. And you could clearly see on the video that their heads were separated from the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The heads had been cut off?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ask Cerkez about HVO shooting with anti-tank rockets at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was his reply?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, his reply was that ask the other side the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What level of concern did he show about the allegations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that he didn't show any concern at all. He was just smiling and I think he was content about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First we got a document that deals with this, which is 895.1. I'm not sure -- perhaps we'll just look at the second sheet, I think. The second fresh paragraph, where it sets out that the team met the commander, HVO Vitez. His main concern was BiH forces from outside still in the area of Kruscica. He stated that digging trenches was no -- explain the following two letters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No ceasefire violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And should not be considered as provocation, but as a normal action during a ceasefire. He had not captured the criminals that forced Muslims out of their houses, nor the soldier who raped women two days ago. Your conclusion was that the ceasefire was not effective today, especially in the area of Kruscica, Vranska and Grbavica; the locals seemed not to obey orders and feel the need to revenge; both sides accused the other in preparing for offensive actions. I wonder if the audio booth could very kindly now play parts 2 and 3 of the same tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the exhibit number of the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three questions arising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I think we were really not able to fully follow what was happening. Could we have the transcript of this video, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can certainly provide one. The position was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript -- I am also interested to see the transcript of -- based on what is heard on the tape, what Cerkez said, because we heard here interpreter, which was probably ECMM interpreter, and it is a clear example of miscommunication. So we should get probably a transcript of Croatian language, not interpreter who is speaking English. It's a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no doubt that can be done. Mr. Nice, perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand. I'm sorry to have -- I apparently wasn't listening. I understand that it's quite difficult to transcribe. We can try again. There are a couple of versions of this tape, and this is the one that has the English translations at its best. And it seemed to us, or certainly seemed to me, that the English half of the communication was certainly clear enough to assist the Chamber. If not in the first hearing, it can always be played again. That, of course, doesn't deal with the possibility of mistranslation between the two people speaking B/C/S or Croatian or whatever proper title for the language is. The problem with the transcript may conceivably be that you are going to have almost too much material. What I suggest we do is try again with the translation department and see if they feel they can provide a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's obviously the first thing to do, and something which is agreed as being the correct translation. And in due course it can be played again, or the transcript can be provided. Clearly, it is important that we should know what the accused actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to insist on also having the transcript in the working languages of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour knows, it's always my concern to ensure that everything that can be said and done in French is said and done in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three questions. Forget the precise terminology used by Mr. Cerkez for the time being. His demeanour, his attitude at this encounter; similar to or different from his attitude on other occasions, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, it's similar to. According to my military point of view, he is responsible for the area. And he is responsible for the ceasefire, he assigned himself, and he doesn't live up to that, and nor do his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second -- sorry. If you had more to say.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If soldiers attack a religious object like a mosque, then the commander is responsible. And he should take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It brings me to my second question. He simply dealt with your query about the attack on the mosque by speaking of the other side. Did you ever get a clear answer as to who was responsible for the attack on the mosque?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And a third matter of detail. The other soldier wearing a blue beret, or the soldier wearing a blue beret, is that a man called Buffini?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will be a witness before the Chamber within the next couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Major, apparently? The U.N. Major you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, a man called Buffini, British, and he is coming along in a couple of weeks' time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, incidentally, if we have trouble dealing with getting a transcript for today's or tomorrow's hearing, it may be that that exercise can be sorted into Buffini's evidence in a week or so's time, because the translation department can't turn around material overnight, particularly if it's difficult to hear. Paragraph 51. On this same day, the 9th of May, did you have a meeting with Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe during the evening, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you've got your own, don't look at the summary, but if you've got your own contemporaneous notes that may help you with the 9th of May, that would be helpful. While the witness is looking that up, it may be convenient if the Court and my learned friends looked towards the back of the bundle to one of the non-statement exhibits or non-typed exhibits, which is a grid paper marked with an organisational diagram. And it's number 253.1. 2535.1. Not the first time I've misquoted an exhibit, and I'm grateful to Mr. Kovacic for telling me at the lunch break that there's a reference I misread and I've got to correct of some sort. Colonel, have you found the reference?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. I found it in my personal diary. But that's in Dutch. So I am pleased to lay it on the ELMO, but I'm afraid nobody can read it. But I am willing to translate it, if needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote down that at 2130, that's half past nine in the evening, there is another meeting. The ambassador tells us that there are very strong signs that the Croats will massively attack on the 11th or the 12th of May. And he states these declaration or declarations made by Mr. Boban and Kordic, and he states this also on the recent attacks on the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what Ambassador Thebault had to say about it all. Did you personally know what kind of declarations that he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He told me that there were radio broadcasts and statements made during meetings in -- that were attended by the ambassador himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just object to this on the grounds of, obviously, hearsay several times removed. But we would have no objections, obviously, to transcripts of the radio broadcasts themselves, if they exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you know we have fairly loose rules as far as hearsay is concerned. It's a matter of weight. There may be other evidence about this. Mr. Nice, are you going to call some other evidence about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the ELMO, there is a diagram. Can you help us with who prepared it and when?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's prepared by the intel. section of the British Battalion in Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first have it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't exactly recall, but I used to visit the intel. section every morning before I went on the ground to hear about certain hot spots and threats, and I was handed this scheme, I think, in the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't necessarily want to go through it at great length because it can speak for itself, but first, did you find it, in your dealings in the territory, accurate, roughly accurate, or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I found it very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find anything that was particularly incorrect in what it described?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. I didn't deal with all the areas as described in this scheme, but the brigades I was dealing with were all accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Starting at the top, it's slightly cut off on all versions, but you can probably explain. "HVO COM in Mostar"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think that's the HVO commander in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Below him is, "Ops Zone, Central Bosnia, Vitez and Travnik," with the commander and deputy commander identified --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- with a solid line leading down to the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Operational Groups?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. The solid lines mean hierarchical lines, so there's a command line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we come one down below the 1st Operational Group, we see horizontal broken lines to the political wing on one side and to the joint commission, Travnik, on the other. Perhaps you would like to explain those in each case.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, it's a difference from the other lines. This dotted line means there's no command structure, at least not a defined command structure. On the left-hand side, you see the political wing and the name of Mr. Kordic, and on the right-hand side, there's the joint command which was signed in the agreement at the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's called a joint commission, in fact?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the joint commission, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the operational groups, on the left, the 1st Operational Group, you've got no names filled for commander and deputy commander there, but below that group, is it, with a solid line, you have "Mario Cerkez" and his brigade or a brigade associated with him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've also got other brigades coming straight off the 1st Operational Group. Who was the commander or deputy commander of the 1st Operational Group, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This structure wasn't fully made clear, since the operational zone had their headquarters in Vitez and the brigade was in Vitez as well, so it was never made clear to us whether there was a specific level in between. It was identified on the right-hand side at the 3rd Operational Group, but not for the 1st and the 2nd Operational Group, so I don't know whether it was intact or it was explained or it was an impression by the intel. officer of the British Battalion. Normally, three crosses on top of the operational zone means army corps level, and in western armies, there's always a division in between the army corps and the brigades, so maybe that's the reason why this intel. officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another possibility is that there was a direct line between the operational zone for Central Bosnia and the brigade commanders identified --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- a few lines down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, in this diagram that we have here, you asked the witness a question, I think, but I didn't quite get the answer. There is a broken line between the political wing of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and we see the name of Kostroman and Dario Kordic and, above that, Mate Boban. Then there is a broken line going towards the operational zone of Central Bosnia. There is no hierarchical relationship, if I understand well, between this political wing and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, of which Mr. Blaskic is the commander, or was there perhaps a hierarchical relationship between the political wing and the military wing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness. I think he used the word "formal", but I'll see what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct; there wasn't a formal hierarchical line, at least not found out by the intel. officer of the British Battalion, but at least it struck me that on the military scheme, the military structure, that the political wing shows up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what way and to what degree, on the basis of your experience, did it have operational control, if any?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I more than once heard commanders refer to things said by Boban or Kordic not officially as an order, but they more or less lived up to those words spoken by Kordic or Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You earlier spoke of the effect on negotiations and, in particular, ceasefire negotiations when the local military commanders were allowed a lesser role and the politicians a greater role?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that stage, what, if any, military command did the politicians appear to exercise?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It was especially in Vitez the case when, at a certain point, the local commanders were no longer attending the local joint commissions, but the politicians came in their place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And yet the outcome of these meetings was something that needed the military to enforce?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, because they always dealt about ceasefire violations, the release of prisoners, freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that goes some way towards answering it through the witness. The issue is generally, of course, one of the issues for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I'm just trying to clarify the answer of the witness regarding the type of relationship that exists. Of course, the Chamber will draw its own conclusions on the basis of all the evidence that will be produced either in the Prosecution or the Defence case. If I understood the witness well, he told us that in the mixed or joint commission, there were politicians most frequently, rather than military men. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the beginning, Your Honour, these local joint commissions -- "local" means just for Vitez or local just for Busovaca -- were only attended by the local commanders from both sides, assisted by their liaison officers. And especially in Vitez, I think starting maybe the second week of May, the whole local joint commission was taken over by the HDZ politicians, Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak and a few others, and the military members did not show up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to finish off this point, in this joint commission, politicians felt capable of making commitments?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They should, if they attended these meetings. But if we started talking about ceasefire violations, then they would say, "No, we can't deal with that. You have to do that separately with the military commanders." So, in fact, the local joint commission was no longer effective as soon as the politicians took on their places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, paragraph 52, did you go to Kiseljak for the first local commission meeting there, nothing being organised, and the HVO commander claiming he was waiting for further orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He didn't deny the existence of prisoners in the Kiseljak barracks. The man Nakic showed some authority and ordered the local commander to form the local commission by the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Members present were Mijo Bosic and Vinko Lucic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 11th of May, paragraph 53, did Cerkez complain about sniper problems at a long and tedious meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that meeting, did you judge the Croats of Vitez willing or unwilling to find a workable solution?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think they became more and more unwilling to support the work of the local joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that in any way relate, in your judgement, to their general state of confidence or in confidence [sic], security or insecurity?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think they felt more and more confidence in their present situation, and I think they more or less reached their goals for that period in that specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, did you go to Kiseljak again, the HVO not showing up, the representatives having to be picked up by Nakic personally, and a ceasefire agreement effective from the following day being reached, with the proposal or the requirement of a list of prisoners dead and missing to be exchanged by that same following day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same 12th of May, did you go to Busovaca joint commission, which resulted in the HVO at Skradno agreeing not to use civilians to dig trenches, it being further confirmed that some prisoners from Kaonik had been released on the previous day, the 11th of May, and brought to Skradno?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know that men held or incarcerated in Kaonik had to dig trenches, some of them being shot and many others wounded?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I was told on that afternoon in Skradno by those people. The people who lived in Skradno or were getting in Skradno and the few released on the day before, they told me, through the interpreter, that they had been forced to dig trenches and that some of their friends or neighbours or relatives got killed during those digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO explanation for this being what?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The HVO commander, Mr. Grubesic, told me that these civilians digging trenches had probably been forced to dig by other civilians and that he was not or he felt not responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to find any support for that allegation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. We checked on that in Skradno, and the people in Skradno told that they were forced to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, two days later, did the local Vitez commission meet, Cerkez present, you telling him to go to the field and see his soldiers if he wants a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. I told him to get control of all his so-called uncontrolled elements, to finally get a real ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had the ABiH released some prisoners by then?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In what area do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, at this time.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They only had a few prisoners in Kruscica, and they already had been released, I think, more than a week before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In this area, was sniping still going on?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a problem particularly with gypsies?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There was a gypsy problem in Kruscica, but both sides seemed not to worry about these people and misused them, and finally UNHCR managed to get this group of gypsies out of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say they both misused them, what did the ABiH do, so far as the gypsies were concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I know I wrote it down somewhere, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if it's in the summary and I can lead it, it's suggested in the summary that they fired on them or at them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I know that I wrote it down somewhere, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that they were used by the HVO to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that both --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make a break between the question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just repeat that answer, please, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that both parties didn't like the group of gypsies and misused them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, did you meet religious leaders in Vitez and also Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have difficulties explaining that murder of civilians was not justified in this area, and was the overall response to that that the problem was caused by Muslim provocation and that -- well, first of all, is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I recall that I got mixed in a real hot discussion about what you can do in wartime and what you can't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was something said about Ahmici itself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, in the whole discussion, it was mentioned that the Muslims caused all the problems themselves and that they called Ahmici upon themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit Z930,1, please. In your daily operational report, second sheet, paragraph 8(B), do you record that the team visited the Catholic leaders in Vitez and met two priests; they seemed to be not fully informed and expressed their own explanations that, "Muslims had provoked HVO several times for the crimes in Ahmici and Old Vitez and even forecast more HVO attacks if the BiH wouldn't stop provoking" or "provocating"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there, in the course of this meeting, any denial of responsibility for Ahmici or Old Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. I don't think these Catholic leaders were responsible themselves, but they didn't deny responsibility from the Croat or HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same day, you went, I think, to Strane to arrange a ceasefire, there being constant fighting in that area. The ceasefire did not succeed, but at that time the HVO appeared to be quite cooperative?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The cooperation was different in various vicinities. In Busovaca, the cooperation was, generally speaking, better than in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 17th of May, a prisoner exchange, Mujahedin against HVO commanders, took place, and as a result, many prisoners were released from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, a meeting of the new local commission of Han Bila, Travnik East, was held at Guca Gora. Two commanders, very cooperative, agreed on a ceasefire, a return of stolen property, the filling of trenches, and freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 61. When you left that meeting, was there heavy mortar and artillery fire directed towards Han Bila?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where from?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: According to our sighting, it came from the area of Vitez, the mountains west of Vitez, Mosul or Mosunj area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under whose control?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This area was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn to paragraph 63, are you aware of a protest from Hadjihasanovic about ceasefire violations at about this time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall the protest itself now. There were a lot of protests from both sides again and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 63. On the 20th of May, was there another local commission meeting in Busovaca, with the HVO reporting ceasefire violations, discussions then being held about prisoner exchange between Busovaca and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The imam from Busovaca attended and complained about local police robbing people and cars and property being taken from civilians?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He had no freedom of movement. They took his car away. They arrested his people when they wanted to go to the mosque. He wasn't free to exercise his religious habits in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll skip 64. Paragraph 65, the 21st of May at the Kiseljak local commission, were there complaints that the HVO had not repaired the power network, the HVO claiming it couldn't be done because of a lack of equipment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the HVO complain about ceasefire violations and shelling; the ABiH replying that they had only responded; Merdan agreeing to find oil and equipment for the power plant; Nakic ordering the commander to stick to the ceasefire agreement?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, did it often enough turn out, as you have told us already, that repair of the power lines was a matter of turning a switch?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Most of the time it was. I think in Kiseljak it was really the damage of a generator station, but in the other areas it was merely switching on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in Exhibit 962. This is the report of the 22nd of May, paragraph 6 headed "Humanitarian." It sets out how the team visited a Muslim community in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finding some 600 Muslims gathered in a few houses, the people not being free to move, despite the HVO denying this fact. Can you help us with how these people were --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Became --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's the same small village of Rotilj I spoke to you about this morning. It's encircled by high mountains and forests. It's a small village in a valley, easily to be sealed off, and it's what's actually sealed off by HVO soldiers. It had a kind of a barrage across the road, so no one could freely enter or leave the village. And I recall that only one or two old women were allowed to leave the village for the few hours to try to find something to eat and to bring it back. But two people can't carry for 600, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 24th of May, paragraph 67: Busovaca local commission reported return of electricity; several shells fired that day. There was a discussion about problems of wounded on both sides, and an agreement was reached to allow representatives from the local commission to visit Zenica prison and the Croat groups in Zenica to check allegations, this visit to be controlled by Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. So representatives of the local commission, Busovaca, were free to go to Zenica to check the allegations they made during previous meetings, so they were able to check them themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same 24th of May, did you visit the Vitez local commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did representatives of the ABiH find themselves held up by a civilian blockade in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. We normally or BritBat normally picked up the members of the local joint commission, since they were not free to move. They had to cross enemy lines several times. So they were picked up by armoured personnel carriers, by the British Battalion, and they were not able to pick the people up and to bring them to this local joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, about the attitude on this day of the defendant Cerkez and what he said.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This blockade was a human blockade by civilians, angry civilians. Later on it was explained to me that they did this because a woman was shot in her back yard and that because of that, people were so angry that they blocked the road to Kruscica. Mr. Cerkez told me that he could not control these civilians and that he was not able to give us a free passage through this blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything else about what he was trying to do at that time and what he might do? And if you have any problems with memory, don't go to the summary, but go to your original notebooks.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall the date again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's not on this one. I have only something in Dutch in my diary, and that is that the situation is completely blocked and that I don't know the way out any more because I cannot control angry women and children myself, and the APCs cannot get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who is this talking? Is this you talking or is this Mr. Cerkez talking?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, this is my own opinion that I wrote down during the night. And finally, after two hours discussions, we have a small step ahead. This commission wants to meet again, but then when both mayors are present. And I state to them that the ceasefire has to be effective because -- or else they have to -- they have to feel themselves responsible for more dead civilians. That's all I can find for now on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's turn to Exhibit 968.1. In the middle of the page, paragraph -- part of paragraph 3, three lines in: "In Kruscica there are approximately 1.500 inhabitants, only five Croat families, of which only two are still in place, and about 3.000 dp's --"

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Displaced persons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- from the west moved in. Also here no PTT comms and a food problem. "HVO has been expelling Muslims from Vitez in all kinds of ways, mostly by threatening the people (extremists). The mayor of Vitez, Mr. Santic, even stated three weeks ago that he would do anything to clean the town of Vitez, just to make room for all Croats bound to come in from Zenica. He even had prepared list of houses that would soon be available. All Muslims from Gacice have been expelled by a group of Croats (HVO?) who told them to leave within 10 minutes. Cattle trucks brought these people to Dubravica, where they were told to walk to Zenica. A similar thing happened in Veceriska. "BiH high-level reps stated their concern that HVO and politicians of the Croat party are working to a certain plan of ethnic cleansing the whole municipality of Vitez. ECMM supports this statement." And over the page at 10, the conclusion: "The situation in and around the Muslim pockets in the area of Vitez is very tense. The 'plan' of ethnic cleansing the area is of great concern. Local commanders seem not to be able to stop fighting. Top-level interference is needed to put proper pressure on the responsible people." Does that reflect the position, as you understood it at that time and from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. That's a special report I wrote on Vitez during that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming back to what, if anything, Mr. Cerkez -- I don't know if you've checked all your records and I'm not sure -- we may not be having a break this afternoon, but if we don't, perhaps you could check them overnight and see if you have any other records of what --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The 24th. I will check. It's a bit mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back, then, to that tomorrow, if sensible, and go to paragraph 69. What was your view of what the HVO's reaction was, particularly insofar as the removal of the blockade is concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: My view was that I could understand that people got angry, civilians got angry because of a woman killed in her back yard, but what I couldn't understand was that according to me, everybody in Vitez supported this blockade and they didn't mind about altogether more than 4.000 people in Kruscica without food. And they didn't mind the freedom of movement for UNHCR or UNPROFOR or ECMM, and they just answered, "Well, it's a civilian problem. It's not our problem. We might not agree with the civilians, but we cannot help you in having freedom of movement." And I still think that the commander -- the man responsible for that area should be able to give us freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find, in the local representatives, a will to make things work?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Not at that time. It took us a long time to get into Kruscica. I think three or four weeks later, we managed for the first time, and we tried every day and got the same answer every day again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, meanwhile, did civilian representatives on both sides agree to meet, in particular Fuad Kaknjo and Munib Kajmovic, being proposed by the HVO as Muslim representatives?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The Muslim side was not able to organise themselves, since they were kept in small pockets, and they couldn't coordinate with each other who to send as a representative. So the HVO side suggested two Muslim representatives, the two names you just mentioned, and those two appeared to us, ECMM, as being just part of the Croat side, although they were Muslims. But they weren't the real representatives of the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 968.1, paragraph 4. Your report for the 24th of May. Sorry. My mistake. Can we move onto the 25th of May. On the 25th of May, did Skopljak, Pero Skopljak, decline or refuse to meet you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He stated that I signed an agreement with him to release all prisoners from Zenica, and he said it was an official document, and since, according to him, I didn't live up to that official agreement, he wasn't willing to meet me any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was what he said true or untrue?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, it was untrue. I did not sign any agreement in releasing prisoners. I couldn't ever release prisoners myself, because I don't have any -- didn't have any prisoners at that time. And the way he explained this agreement was signed, it was clear to me that I could never have done it myself, since he used my full Christian name, and in the Netherlands we don't sign with full Christian names. So I didn't believe this document to be true, and I couldn't remember anything being signed by myself. But the Ambassador took it very serious, Mr. Thebault, and he said, "Well, you will not go to Vitez for the first few days," since he thought it could be dangerous for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So instead you went to a provincial civil government planning meeting in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, did you meet with military commanders in the joint command in Travnik, they showing determination to fight the Serbs and not each other, and agreeing to implement the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, at the local Busovaca commission where ceasefire violations were reported, the HVO representatives being in Zenica -- I'm sorry, they visited Zenica, and that was satisfactory, was it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a problem with drunken HVO soldiers in the area, or apparently a problem?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This occurred more than once, these claims that drunken soldiers had misbehaved themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you recover two bodies of elderly men from a minefield in Strane later that day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. Alongside the Lasva River there were two dead bodies. These two old men tripped on two mines approximately one week before and they couldn't be evacuated, so we had to arrange a ceasefire, had to find soldiers who were able and willing to get these dead bodies out of the minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you visit Vitez the same day, where there was still shooting, meeting Santic, Skopljak and Cerkez, with whom a political discussion developed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was said about the prospects for an army of joint command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They did no longer believe in a joint military or civil life. They discussed a lot about the Vance-Owen Plan, about the borders. They -- especially Mr. Santic, he told me that in the beginning the Vance-Owen Plan could not be implemented the way it was signed, it should be altered. Local politicians were not asked for their opinion about the Vance-Owen Plan, so they were not able to implement it. They should have been asked before, and they suggested all kinds of changes in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was anything said specifically about what should happen to the territory of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Vitez should be purely Croats, and it should be demilitarised. That was the suggestion of Santic and Skopljak. Demilitarised, the whole area, withdrawal of all troops, and then arrangements could be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also meet on this day the mayor of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His name being --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you meet him? What was said?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the -- I met him in the town hall in Busovaca. I remember that very precise, since I only been once inside the town hall. All the other meetings were always held in the Dutch Battalion headquarters. And Mr. Maric told me that the HDZ side had already chosen representatives for the provincial level from the -- referring to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "the provincial level," how is that defined or identified?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the whole area there were three provinces that were important, 8, 9 and 10, and I don't exactly know what province is in what area. But Busovaca/Vitez is in one province, and Travnik is in the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What personalities were identified?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The same names that showed up every time, the names of Kordic, Santic, Skopljak, and a few others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These people would have what position?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They would have -- they were suggested to become the political leaders on the provincial government level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having visited Busovaca, Vitez and -- Busovaca and Vitez, did you return to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have contact with the SDA in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, if that's in your notebooks. It hasn't been challenged, but I don't want to take you to the summary unless it's definitely accurate.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: What date is that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe you can look at your summary for speed. Paragraph 75. The 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I recall now speaking to the SDA because I remember -- because I got the names from the HDZ side, I tried to get names from the SDA side as well. But they couldn't organise themselves, so they were not prepared to give the names of their representatives at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Skopljak made a claim?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but I have to look at the outline again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact. The problem was that if they tried to organise in the Vitez area, I mean the SDA side, then they should be free to move. They should meet each other, and in this meeting they could assign representatives. And then Skopljak said, "Well, I am not able to guarantee their safety." And the result of that was that the SDA people never met in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 992.1. Your note or report for the 28th of May. Paragraph 4 deals with tripartite meetings and sets out that eventually both parties, you say, HDZ and SDA, accept the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say, "Mr. Santic stated the HDZ is ready to implement it, but that he thinks it not wise to do so." And you record a discussion. And it's just maybe worth the Chamber noting that four lines up from the bottom of this paragraph, "The SDA made a precondition to exchange the family of Dr. Mujezinovic, a former leader of the Muslims in Vitez, to a HVO soldier captured in Poculica". Paragraph 76. Did you, on this same day, meet with the presidency and military representatives of the provincial government at Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any progress made with a joint police force?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. They had large problems in this police force. It consisted of both civil and military police, and then military police from both parties, HVO and army ABiH. They didn't trust their assigned chief of police and they had big problems in mixed patrols and mixed police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ask Blaskic to establish something about the imprisonment of four people said to be kept at --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. The request during that meeting was made to release four people, four Muslim people from Travnik. And I handed over this request to Blaskic himself, and according to my knowledge, these people were never released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And 997.1. The operational report from two days later in paragraph 1 sets out how the situation in the area of Travnik was tense, since as at the 28th four Muslims were taken to Busovaca prison and one HVO military policeman had been killed, three Croat members of the presidency and government of Travnik arrested. Are those separate incidents from the detention of the four people in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, as such, they were separate, but they were a reaction. But the three Croats were released after our negotiations, and the four Muslims were never -- according to my knowledge, were not released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment? Where have you got to; paragraph 78?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 78. Before I pass, while we're on today's transcript still, I'm told that I have misquoted or misidentified two exhibits. I'm grateful to the Registry for the second, which is that what I've identified as Exhibit 930,1, a videotape, was already admitted and that it should be marked as 930,2. Then Mr. Kovacic has been good enough to advise me that I had simply misread a number right at the beginning in relation to the map, I think, and the map is Z2175, and I think I transposed two of those numbers. The only map that's been produced today is 2175. Copies of the missing exhibit, special report of the 4th of May, Exhibit Z882, are now available for inclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, would you be back, please, at half past 9.00 tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of October, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
